subtopic: ORDER IN COUNCIL TRANSMITTED TO IMPERIAL GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ORDER IN COUNCIL TRANSMITTED TO IMPERIAL GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
i beg to lay on the table of the House an Order in Council passed on the * 15th instant. As it relates to a subject that has been under discussion in the House recently it may be proper that I should read it:
Upon a memorandum from the Right Honourable the Prime Minister, dated the 13th day of April, 1916, touching a motion by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in the House of Commons on the 7th day of March, 1916, in the following terms:
" That a special committee of 

 member of this House be appointed to inquire into all purchases of shells or other munitions or goods by the Shell Committee formed by the Minister of Militia, as stated to this House by the Prime Minister on the 15th April, 1915, together with all contracts made or orders given by the said committee for any shells or other munitions or goods, with authority to the said committee to examine witnesses under oath and to require the production of any documents, books, letters or papers; and that such special committee be directed to report from time to time to this House in such manner as it may think advisable."
The Prime Minister calls attention to his own remarks in the House of Commons in speaking upon this motion, in which he made the following statement:
" Now, what course does the Government propose to take with regard to the motion which my right hon. friend has proposed to this House? As far as the Shell Committee is concerned- I shall speak afterwards of another matter- our proposal is this:	We shall direct the attention of the British Government in detail to every charge, allegation and rumour brought up in this House or elsewhere by my right hon. friend or by any of his supporters with regard to the Shell Committee. We shall further inform the British Government that if an inquiry is thought advisable, we are prepared to cooperate with them to the fullest extent, and to issue any commission, take any proceedings, pass any legislation, and do any other act for the purpose of making that inquiry as full, thorough, and complete as they deem advisable. But without their consent or approval, we do not propose to enter upon an investigation or inquire into such expenditures by the British Government."
The Prime Minister further observes that the expenditure made by the Shell Committee (so-called) was on behalf of the Government ol the United Kingdom, and was not on behalf of the Government of Canada; and that the Government of Canada did not fix or determine the prices to be paid for shells contracted for by the Shell Committee.
Having regard to these considerations and to the statement above quoted, the Prime Minister recommends that the Hansard report of the debate upon the motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier be transmitted , to the Right Honourable the Secretary of State for the Colonies, with the assurance that the Government of Canada is prepared to assist and co-operate, as stated by the Prime Minister in the House of Commons, in any inquiry or investigation into the transactions to which reference is made in the motion

of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and that so far as the Government of Canada is concerned there is no objection whatever to the fullest investigation that may be thought desirable at any time.
The Prime Minister further recommends that a copy of the Order in Council approved on the 3rd instant which authorizes the issue of a Royal Commission to the. Honourable Sir William Ralph Meredith, Chief Justice of Ontario, and the Honourable Lyman Poole Duff, one of the Justices of the Supreme Court of Canada be also transmitted to the Right Honourable the Secretary of State for the Colonies for the information of the Government of the United Kingdom.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendation and submit the same for approval.
(Sgd.) Rodolphe Boudreau,
Clerk of the Privy Council.

1.	Do the existing: laws permit the naturalization of aliens of enemy nationality?
2.	If so, what number of such persons, if any, have been naturalized in Canada since the beginning of the present war?
3.	Is it the intention of the Government to introduce such legislation as will render it impossible for any person of enemy nationality to become naturalized during the period of the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
X. Under the Naturalization Act of 1914, the granting of certificates of naturalization is discretionary with the Secretary of State. The policy of not granting such certificates to persons of alien enemy nationality in the exercise of that discretion has been adopted.
Under the Naturalization Act of 1870, continued in force for a period of three years from the 1st January, 1915, for aliens resident in Canada before that date, and under which exclusive Canadian nauraliza-tion is granted, the granting of certificates is in the hands of the judges. The decisions of the courts differ upon the question as to whether the state of war suspends the operation of this Act as regards persons of alien enemy nationality.
2.	As the entire list of persons of all nationalities naturalized since the beginning of the war has to be gone through to pick out those of alien enemy nationality, it will take considerable time before the information is available; it will be brought down* as soon as procured.
3.	At the outset of the war, the Government by proclamation, announced to persons of alien enemy nationality that so long as they quietly pursue their ordinary avocations they would be allowed to continue to enjoy the protection of the law and be accorded the respect and consideration due to peaceful and law-abiding citizens. In view of the large number of persons of alien enemy nationality who have proved themselves to be absolutely peaceable and not dangerous, and who had taken up homesteads under a law providing that upon the expiry of three years they would be entitled to the naturalization qualifying then to obtain patents to their lands, and of the fact that in the opinion of the Government, no serious injury is to be apprehended from leaving the Act of 1870 so temporarily in force, to such operation as

the courts may recognize it to have in the case of alien enemies, it is not intended to modify that Act.

There is included in these papers a resolution of the Selkirk Board of Trade in regard to St. Peters reserve. The resolution is so very lengthy that I will not trouble the House to read it all, but the introduction to the resolution, not being so long, I may be permitted to read it: Selkirk, Man., Feb. 11.
At the annual meeting of the Selkirk Board of Trade a week ago, a resolution 'on the St. Peters question, which was being concurrently passed by the municipal councils of St. Clements, St. Andrews, and the town of Selkirk, was laid on the table, and in accordance with a motion passed at that time, the new council of the board were instructed to prepare and pass a, resolution of endorsement, which they did last night as the first official act of their body.
Both the municipal resolution and that of the Board of Trade are uncompromising in their attitude toward the further delay that will be inevitable as a result of the motion now entered in the Exchequer Court by the Government, and the municipal resolution bluntly asks for a confirmation of the original surrender by the present Parliament.
People who are not directly interested in this controversy can hardly realize the disappointments the people of Selkirk have suffered in their eight-year effort to secure settlement of the surrender, which, the Board of Trade complains, has done far more damage in the community by reason of its delay, than the direct issue involved could ever amount to. The resolution of the Board is a striking resume of eight years of untiring effort met with fair promise, and balked by mysterious opposition.
A resolution by the St. Clements municipal council is included in these papers, and with the permission of the House I will read a portion of that resolution:
We emphatically protest against this suit. That is, the suit in the Exchequer Court.
In the first place, whether the final judgment of the courts be for or against the validity of the surrender, the great delay necessarily involved in securing such final judgment would be unfair to this municipality, intolerably unfair when added to the already unwarranted, delay in starting the suit.
Secondly, if the final judgment should set aside the surrender, then a further period of delay would be added for negotiating a fresh surrender and arranging and carrying out allotments and issuing fresh patents consequent thereon. After the past delay, we are surely entitled to some quicker mode of settlement than this.
In the third place, if this surrender is set aside, it is extremely doubtful if another surrender should be negotiated or secured at all,

and for this territory to again become, or to continue indefinitely as an Indian reserve, would be nothing short of a calamity to this municipality, economically and socially as well as financially.
Fourthly and lastly, the grounds set forth in the said suit (the writ of information in which has been read by this council) are purely technical in their nature and consists of alleged irregularities upon tlic part of the Government officials concerned in the surrender and in no way whatever charge any blame against the1 defendants, the present holders of the titles. Under the circumstances, even if the grounds of the suit are true in fact and sufficient in law (as to which, of course, we express no opinion), they are of such a nature as to clearly call (on public grounds) not for cancellation of the surrender, but the very opposite, namely, its confirmation. If such confirmation calls for compensation to the Indians (as to which we express no opinion) then the Governm nt, whose officials committed the alleged irregularities should surely make such compensation.
Now, therefore, for these reasons, this municipality in its corporate capacity, hereby urges and demands, as the quickest and most equitable and satisfactory mode of settlement of the question, that the surrender be confirmed by the proper governmental or legislative authorities without further delay.

Hereby resolves: that as a body representative of the entire community and district we are firmly convinced that the common injury and injustice being wrought by the hold-up of these lands from occupation, has created a situation, the continuance of which would be intolerable.
Further, that the Indians as a body are, and always have been, fully satisfied with the surrender and its terms.

So that, in view of the fact that Chief Justice Howell, who had been so prominent in connection with the negotiations, after the surrender had been made, should have found it incumbent upon him to advise the registrar general of Manitoba not to issue Torrens titles until he was satisfied that the Indians were properly dealt with; I say in view of that fact, my hon. friend should not have blamed the registrar general for being alarmed and refusing to issue those titles, because the registrar general was the custodian of the guarantee fund which exists in Manitoba to guarantee every title that is issued; and the registrar general knew his responsibility to tho Government and to the province; he



knew that if anything was found wrong with those titles; he knew that if they could be successfully attacked, the province of Manitoba would be responsible and would have to make good the difference between the price the lands were sold at and their proper value. In view of that fact, this was, to say the least, extravagant language for my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) to have used in reference to Mr. Miaoara.
My friend harks back to the old ques-iton of the surrender-was it legal or not legal? That is the whole question, aside from the fact of the fraud being committed by the purchasers. That phase of the question has never been gone into, it has never been brought before the court; and it is not intended in the Bill now before the House to deal with that question. The whole question was the legality or the illegality of the surrender. If the surrender was legal, there would have been no doubt at all about the purchasers being able to force Mr. Macara to accept those titles.
Now, what took place? It was, I think, in 1907, that this surrender was taken. The matter hung from 1907 until 1911, the year of the defeat of the late Government. Time after time this matter was brought before Parliament, and I myself, from my place, urged the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) to institute an investigation. I laid what I conceived to be the clearest possible kind of evidence. of wrong-doing in connection with this surrender before this House; but I received no encouragement from my hon. friend or from his friends. They refused even to investigate. My hon. friend answered that there was nothing to investigate, that the Government had accepted the surrender, that the lands had been disposed of, and that the surrender was final. According to my hon. friend, the Indians were perfectly satisfied with that surrender, but, as a matter of fact, they were the parties who drew my attention to the rascality of the transaction. Letter after letter, affidavit after affidavit were placed on Hansard from these men asking for justice, and showing the manner in which they had been treated, but I received no encouragement from my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver), and he would do nothing but state that there was nothing to investigate. A royal commission was appointed. Why was it appointed? It was appointed at the request of a large body of the Indians who petitioned the Provincial Government. They had exhausted their powers to induce the men who were in 
office prior to 1911 to intervene on their behalf to protect them. They had exhausted their patience in trying to get my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), who was responsible, as Minister of Indian Affairs, for the care of those Indians, to intervene; consequently, they appealed to the Provincial Government. They claimed that they had been defrauded out of their lands, and the Provincial Government, for its own protection, and for the protection of the titles, so that the Registrar General might not be led into any mistake, appointed a commission. That commission consisted of three county judges, Judges Meyars, Prudhomme and Lock. These judges took volumes of evidence; they sat day after day in Selkirk, and day after day in Winnipeg, and every available witness who could throw any light on the question of the legality of the surrender was examined. The evidence was, as I have said, voluminous, and after it had been concluded and summed up, two of the judges, Judge Lock and Judge Prudhomme, reported that the surrender was illegal and void, and could not have been anything else from the beginning. Judge Meyars signed a minority report; he did not agree with the finding of the two other judges. But the fact that two judges decided that the transaction was illegal ought surely to have settled the question as to the legality of the transaction.
But one has only to read the Indian Act to find out that the surrender was illegal. The Indian Act provides that a majority of the male members of the band, over 21 years of age, are entitled to vote, and, it is the interpretation of that clause which has been in dispute between my hon. friend and myself. The interpretation placed upon it by the Indian Department during the regime of my hon. friend was that it meant a majority of the Indians who assembled at a meeting. That will strike every man as a most absurd proposition. I think there were some 250 or 260 votes in the band-I forget exactly how many-^but say there were only 50 Indians assembled; would it not be absurd to say that those 50 men could alienate all the rights and interests of the other members of the band who were not present? I put that question to my hon. friend when the matter was formerly under discussion, and his answer was that they would have the legal right to alienate the lands* but perhaps not the moral right. I am not going to argue this question; I do not wish to open up another debate upon

it; but it does seem to me that, in view of what has taken place, in view of the evidence that was taken by the commission, and in view of Chief Justice Howell's decision, the men who negotiated the surrender in going to Mr. Macara showed that they had doubts as to the manner in which the Indians had been treated. Nobody can read the evidence without seeing in every line of it a determined effort on the part of Mr. Pedley and those who were interested to secure that surrender by any means. There is no question about that. The meeting was called on one day's notice. I have gone into all this before. One day's notice was given to a band of Indians living on a reserve 50 miles square, many of whom were out on the lake fishing. The result was that when the meeting was called dozens and dozens of the voters were absent. Some of them did not hear about the surrender for weeks after the meeting had taken place. The meeting was held in a small building, and half of those in attendance could not get in to hear the terms of the surrender. That is brought out dozens of times in the evidence. Another important point is that the terms of surrender were not read to the Indians in their own language; dozens of the Indians who were present did not understand the terms. In view of these facts, it is not surprising that the commission was appointed to ascertain whether the surrender was legal or otherwise. If the surrender was not legal, nothing else attached to it meant anything. My hon. friend from Edmonton knows, as well as I do, that if the men whoi secured those lands in the first place had felt aggrieved and thought that they had good ground to stand upon in regard to the legality of the surrender, they would not have hesitated to take a case to court. I had a conversation with Mr. Macara himself in 1909-10, I think. The case' was dragging on, and people were urging a settlement, and I asked what he wanted to enable him to issue the titles. He said to me, " I will be satisfied either with an Act of Parliament, or with the judgment of any court in Manitoba." I told those gentlemen, I told Mr. Andrews, who was acting for them: " If you are so. sure of your ground why not take one of ,the cases to court and endeavour to compel Mr. Macara to issue a title. Macara says that when you do that, he will accept the judgment of the court, and will issue a title to every one of those patents." But they did not do that. Why? I do not think 184J

However, the Bill that is before the House is more in the shape of a compromise than anything else. I want to be frank with the House and the country and I want to say that I do not consider-that I have never considered-it to be an equitable settlement of this affair. The Indian, I believe, to-day, just as I believed six or seven years ago, has been cheated out of a very valuable asset. There is no question about that in my mind. This is a compromise measure, and it is a compromise simply because the matter was allowed to drag year after year until dozens and hundreds of innocent people became involved. When I first brought this matter before the House and asked for an investigation, and for legislation, very few were affected who were not the original pur-

chasers, and the original purchasers were the people who ought to have suffered at that time if anybody ought to' have suffered. As time went on, dozens and hundreds of innocent people became purchasers of this land. I need not say that I was amazed at the statement made by my hon. friend, because I suppose my hon. friend wishes in the dying days of the discussion of this matter-probably this is the last time it will come before this House and the House will not be sorry-to justify not only his own act but the acts of the Administration of which he was not an unimportant member at that time. The transaction bore on the face of it an attempt to deceive the public. You will remember, Sir, that the settlement was that each member of the Indian family got 16 acres. If a man had a wife he sometimes got 32 acres. Some of these Indians were induced by unscrupulous men to sign a document purporting to be an agreement of sale, and that, in many instances, constituted a statutory deed of the man's property. Time after time men have told me that they received nothing for their lands. I do not wish to recite all these things, as it is late in the day now, but in view of these facts I think my hon. friend from Edmonton, who is more responsible than any other man for this matter, was ill-advised to make the statement he did regarding the acceptance of these titles by the Registrar General of Manitoba. While I am not prepared to say that this settlement is doing the Indians anything

like justice, I do say that I think that perhaps it is wise, in view of all the circumstances, to accept the settlement provided . in this Bill. Mr. Macara did not refuse to register those surrenders.

That is what I understand.

What he Teads-and it
is exactly as I recall the words of the minister-is that the Registrar General had stated that if the assurance of the Government were given that legislation of this character would be-introduced as a Government measure, he would be prepared to act as though it were passed and ratify the title. Whether or not there have been cases before him, and he has issued titles, I 3o not know, and consequently cannot state. But he did agree that if the promise were given by the Government to introduce legislation-and it was-he would be in a position to, and would, ratify the title.
How could he do that? How could he give a legal title?
Because it would become legal by this legislation; and because the Registrar General, like most people, ha. confidence that legislation introduced by this Government will pass.
Does that follow?

I say they have confidence that it will pass. And I think that the hon. member for St. John has learned in the past five years to have the same confidence, if he would only acknowledge it. It is for the Registrar General to de-

cide; and he had sufficient confidence,- doubtless backed by the confidence of the present' Government of Manitoba,-and the joint confidence of these two institutions brought them 'to the conclusion that they would be quite safe in acting upon the promise of the present minister to introduce legislation.
May I ask for information, does the Registrar General of Manitoba a< on his own responsibility in registering, or does he share responsibility with the Government of Manitoba?

That is something which my hon. friend might appeal to the Government of Manitoba to answer. The Registrar General is not an official of this Government, but of the Government of Hon. Mr. Norris in Manitoba. How far they interfere with his administration of his office I have no means of knowing.
Then his office is not strictly judicial?

In part judicial, I should think. I should, say that the Government under which he acts could make it his duty to register titles if they wished to do so, by means of legislation, and if they are not satisfied they could appoint somebody else.
And they could prevent him from registering, as the Roblin Government did.

I do not know that the Roblin Government ever interfered, and never heard that they did, but I do know that the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal of Manitoba made his recommendation, as did two other judges, which was acted upon.
Which, of course, was none of his business; he- had no interest in the matter, near or remote.

I did not observe any action taken by the late administration to correct that judge in the discharge of his duty. What I set out to say was that the legislation as it at present stands makes the surrender legal, conditional upon the payment of $1 an acre, or the giving of a lien for that amount. The legislation as proposed to be amended would make it legal without any payment whatever. Now, the hon. member for Edmonton says that, even in its present form as introduced by the Government, it amounts to an instruction to the Registrar General to legalize the titles without payment.

I do not know that I understand it to te an instruction to the Registrar General. I think by the questions I asked my hon. friend (Mr. -Meighen), and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) it was demonstrated that the Registrar General for Manitoba was not under the instructions of this Government.
What the hon. gentleman said was that the effect of the legislation as introduced made it the duty of the Registrar General, if he was -an honest man, to pass the title without payment.
Not as an instruction.

Made it his duty, if he was an honest man. Then, why does the hon. gentleman introduce an amendment to make it his duty to pass the title without payment? There can be only one answer, and that is, that he has no confidence in the Registrar General.

The hon. gentleman insists on misrepresenting the expression I used in regard to the relationship of the Registrar General to the legislation proposed by the Government. He would make it appear that I had said that this legislation was a direction to the Registrar General, or that he was expected to act on it.

What the hon. gentleman said is on record. He agreed with me that I interpreted it correctly when I said that its effect at present was to make it the duty of the Registrar General, if he is an honest man, to pass the title without-
Not as a direction.

That is the way I represented it the last three times. Its- effect is to make it his duty, if he is an honest man, to pass the title without payment. Why, th(en, does the hon. gentleman introduce an amendment asking us to plainly say in the Act that he must pass the title without payment? That would make its effect in his view exactly as it is now.
Yes.

Then, his amendment
is, even in his own opinion, no amendment at all, and merely brings out the reason why he moves it, which is, that he has no confidence in the Registrar General. Well, the Registrar Gfeneral can be made to do this by legislation of the Government of Manitoba. So the hon. gentleman's lack of confidence must cover both the Government of

Manitoba and the Registrar General. And that is the whole basis of his amendment.
However, the effect of the Bill at present is not at all to make it the duty of the Registrar General to pass the title without payment, but to pass it upon payment of $1 an acre, or upon the filing of a lien for that amount. I do not think it would be well for this House to consider an amendment ratifying the surrender and procuring in the settlement nothing at all for the wards of this Government. I think it is the duty of the Government to procure all we can for the wards of the Government, and to procure it from those who profited by the illegality brought about by the late Government.
It is cbntended that all the records show, and that the petitions read by the hon. member for Edmonton show, that the surrender in the first place was in the interest of the Indians themselves, and in the interest of the country. I do not argue and I do not think it has ever been argued, that the taking of a surrender, were it properly done, was not in the interests of the Indians and of the country.	The taking of a surrender may well have been in the interests of the Indians and in the interests of the country if such were properly and legally done and if justice were done the wards of the Government in the method adopted and in the general execution of the project. All that has been contended is this: That in the method adopted and in the execution of the project, the interests of the wards of the Government were not conserved. Now, we set about to remedy that state of affairs; we issue a writ in the Exchequer Court asking for the cancellation of the surrender. It is urged by the hon. member for Edmonton that there is nothing in the writ ascribing fraud on the part of those who purchased after the surrender was effected and at the auction sale. That is correct, but why would that be necessary in a writ such as this? The surrender is called in question; the whole method of obtaining that surrender is declared to' be fraudulent from the beginning, not merely illegal in that the majority did not consent, but fraudulent in that bribery was indulged in for the purpose of getting it-wrong pressure and wrong promises. If that is established; if the Government's contention is right, then the whole thing is upset and the auction sale falls down with it, and every-
[ Mr. Meishen.]
thing falls. Consequently, the information in the Exchequer Court goes the full length that it needs to go; to go further would be surplusage in the present action. It does not at all admit that in the auction sale which followed tfte wards of the Government were protected as they should have been protected by the Government of the day.
The hon. member should see that what the petitions urge is this: Inasmuch as all this, right or wrong, was done by a Government or by a Government official, the people of Canada should stand by it. That is what the petitions urge. They say that Mr. Pedley may have done wrong or he may	have done
right; he may have committed fraud or he, may have been an honest man. But whatever he did, he was your official; he was the official of the Government of Canada;1 consequently we call upon you to make good what he did.	That is the
attitude taken by the petitions, but that is far from arguing, as the hon. member from Edmonton did, that the methods adopted were right in themselves.
We have effected a settlement which means the restitution of about $40,000 to the wards of this Government; we have brought this penalty upon those who profited by the transaction. We cannot bring the penalty upon the late Government; the people of Canada are the only people who could do that, and they have done it in so far as it was in their power The late Government are the other parties who did wrong, and we cannot possibly compensate for their wrong; we cannot possibly visit any penalty upon them The only ones we can get it from are those who profited by it, and we do so to the'extent of the sum stipulated in the Bill.
I do not want to cover the ground again, but let me point this out: the hon. member for Edmonton read the contentions of the counsel for these parties, the defendants. To put forward the contention from the point of view of counsel that these persons bought in good faith, and all the rest of it, does not by any means say that his contention is correct or founded on fact; he is arguing that as lawyer for these defendants. It would have been fair, I think, had the hon. gentleman also put on record my reply, in which, while accepting on behalf of the Government the terms suggested, I clearly stipulated that it was no admission on our part that the surrender had itself been legal or that the proceedings that were

part of the surrender were not fraudulent. I do not wish to read the whole of the letter, as it is rather long, but I shall read one short paragraph. The letter is dated June 8, 1915, addressed to Messrs. Andrews, Andrews & Co., and signed by myself:
Such acceptance as is herein set out is not decided upon by reason of any change of view on the part of this department or of the Government as to the legality of the surrender now in question or as to the propriety of the proceedings that led to and that followed the surrender. We are disposed to view favourably a settlement by reason of considerations arising out of difficulties that are necessarily entailed by the unsettled conditions of titles to so large an amount of land and the consequent retardation of settlement in the district concerned. These results in turn affect many who are innocent of all connection with the original proceedings-affect indeed the Indians themselves and the public generally.
There is succinctly stated the position originally assumed and maintained by the Government, and, furthermore, the reasons why it is impossible to bring home to the parties the due penalty for the wrongs they committed. It is impossible to bring home to the Government of that day a penalty for the wrong it committed; for that I am very sorry. It is impossible to bring home to the parties who received the benefits of the wrongs committed the punishment that they deserve in each case.. To do so would involve the very disasters that are pointed out in the petitions read by the hon. member for Edmonton-the retardation of settlement, the closing of school districts, the holding back of land development and the penalizing of those who innocently secured titles afterwards. That is the whole basis and cause of settlement. It does not pretend to do full or substantial justice to the Indians; such is impossible by reason of the considerations that arose afterwards, and in the hands of which we were not able to do that substantial justice. It does not pretend to do that, but it pretends to go as far along the road of substantial justice as it is practicable and possible to go at the present distance of time.

I think that my
hon. friend	has	forgotten to tell
the House one very important thing, and [DOT] that is that it was he himself who gave the assurance by letter that the Government would introduce legislation, and he gave that assurance with a view to inducing the Registrar of Titles to pass favourably upon the titles and to issue the necessary certificates. The certificates of title issued so far as those who
were paying cash was concerned would give absolutely good title, I may say to the hon. member for Selkirk, whether this legislation passes or does not pass, because under the Land Titles Act a certificate of title issued by the registrar is absolutely good and cannot be questioned by any one. Of course, if anybody should have a claim by reason of his title having been taken away from him, that claim -would be against the fund which is paid into the treasury under the Land Titles Act.
As I understand the hon. member for Edmontbn, what he complains of is this: the correspondance, beginning with the letter of Mr. Norquay, who is a leading Conservative in Manitoba, and who appears to be manager of an important real estate company, and the resolutions of the various municipal councils, show that there is no evidence whatever that there was an irregularity or any wrong-doing of any kind or description in connection with the disposal of the land in this reserve. This land having been disposed of away back in the year 1908 and this Government having now by their action admitted that no fraud was perpetrated, that no one was guilty of any wrong-doing, and that the matter should be settled and . the titles made * absolutely good, the contention of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is that it is entirely wrong, that these purchasers, who paid their money eight years ago into the treasury of the country, and who obtained what they thought was their title to these properties, should now be called upon to pay to the Government the sum of $1 per acre additional, in order to prevent themselves from being held up, and in order to secure their deeds. That is what my hon. friend complains of, arid is that not a correct position to take? Is this Government so much in need of .money that it must hold up these people, and, by pointing the gun at them, say to them: "No matter how innocent you may be, we are determined to carry this case to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, unless you pay into the treasury of Canada the sum of $1 per acre." My hon. friend the Solicitor General is compelled to admit that there are men who have bought the lands in this reserve who are absolutely innocent purchasers, who paid their money in good faith;, that there are people like the widow of the man to whom my hon. friend from Edmonton has referred, whose husband

bought this land .in good faith .and paid his purchase price to the Government. The Solicitor General is compelled to admit that the innocent and the guilty, as he calls them, are being treated alike, that these people are compelled to pay money which they have no right to pay; and this the hon. member for Edmonton says, and so do I, on the evidence we have submitted, is an injustice of the worst possible kind that is being inflicted upon innocent people.
I admit that this Government was standing between the devil and the deep sea when it came into power. There was the hon. member for 'Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), who had been for years declaiming in this Parliament, for political effect-

Nothing else.
Mr. PU'GSLEYthat a great wrong had been perpetrated against these Indians-

That is right.
. Mr. PUGSLEYthat an enormous wrong had been perpetrated against them. The Government came into power in 1911 when, if there had been this wrong, it was the duty of the Government to deal with it. But they did not deal with it, they took no step of any kind or description for the first three years they were in 5 p.m. office, until 1914, when people 'began to complain of the long delay, of the inaction of the Government, and of the fact that these titles were being held up; that industries were prevented from being started on lands in connection with this reserve. And then comes a letter from this prominent Conservative, Mr. Norquay, addressed to the Prime Minister, in which he says that the.Hon. Dr. Montague, the Minister of Public Works in the Manitoba Government, was running an election in this constituency, and that unless there was some assurance that this matter would be settled it would operate most disadvantageous^ to Dr. Montague and the Conservative party, both in Manitoba and at Ottawa, if the matter was not speedily settled. Mr. Norquay also says that it is going to affect Mr. Bradbury-
So it will; it will give me the biggest majority I ever had.

It is going to affect Mr. Bradbury if it is not settled; and at last, in winding-up, he tells the Prime Minister that Liberals and Conservatives have both invested in these lands, that it is an enormous hardship. And then he separates the 
Conservative party from the people of Manitoba, and he says it is of great importance to tire people of Manitoba, as well as to the Conservative party. Let me read the letter.
It was of greater interest to Mr. Norquay than to the people of Manitoba.

Mr. Norquay? Mr. Norquay's name is a good Conservative name in Manitoba. This is what he says:
This surrender was made under a commission issued to the hon. Chief Justice Howell.
A man whom I think the Government could fairly trust to do justice so far as the Indians were concerned. Then Mr. Norquay says:
To continue delay in settling this question, cannot but be attended with results inimical to our party here and in Ottawa, and in the interests of our member, Mr. George Bradbury, no better act could be done on his behalf than to place him in a position whereby he may receive the unanimous support of the party which at the present time is endangered by the fact that not only Liberals, but Conservatives as wen have purchased these lands and the monies are hid up until a settlement is effected.
And he winds up with an expression of his sincere trust that the Prime Minister will give personal attention to this matter, and that his personal attention will produce the result of relieving the Manitoba Government of the incubus of retarded development, and, thereby earning the gratitude of the people and the Conservative party in Manitoba.
The Prime Minister does not dispute these statements of Mr. Norquay. He apparently admits the truth of them, because if he had reason, after three years in office, to believe that Mr. Norquay was not stating what was true when he alleged that the grantees were entitled to their patents, that they had bought the lands and paid for them, and were entitled to get their deeds, the Prime Minister would naturally have replied to Mr. Norquay that there was fraud in connection with this matter, and that the Government could not act upon his recommendation. The Prime Minister writes to the Solicitor General, and he tells him that he has informed Mr. Norquay that the suggestions which Mr. Norquay had made would receive " the careful and earnest consideration of the Government." Those suggestions, of Mr. Norquay were very important to the Conservative party, very important to this Government, because Mr. Norquay is calling the attention of the Government to their inexcusable delay in

settling this matter. They had succeeded in 1908, apparently through their Conservative friends in their Manitoba Government, in preventing the Registrar General of Titles from issuing the certificates of title which it was his duty to do under the sales which had taken place. The matter had 'been held up for three years pending the coming into office of this Government, and for three years longer they remained inactive, and, Sir, we can only believe that they remained inactive because they felt that there was no ground on which action could be taken to set aside these sales upon the pretext of fraud or irregularity. But when at length the fact is impressed upon them by Mr. Norquay that this is of vast importance1 to Dr. Montague, the Minister of Public Works in Manitoba, who is running an election, that it is of vast importance to Mr. Norquay, who will not get a corporal's guard of the electors unless this is settled, and that it is of enormous importance to the Conservative party of Manitoba-this wakens up the Prime Minister, and he writes a letter to Mr. Meighen, in which he says he has assured Mr. Norquay that his suggestions, which are all along political lines, will receive the earnest and careful consideration of the Government. But see the position the Government were in in relation to their very warm supporter, their very loyal friendi, the member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury). They could not allow the thing to go by the board, they could not confirm the titles, because that would discredit the hon. member for Selkirk; that would be telling the people of Manitoba that he had no ground for making these charges, session after session, in this Parliament. So the ingenuity of my hon. friend' the Solicitor General is called upon to devise a way by means of which the people of Selkirk can be satisfied, and by means of which the political scalp of the hon. member for Selkirk may be saved to himself.
It is quite safe.

And so they devised this extraordinary scheme, by means of which the sum of $1 per acre is to be paid by these people towards the .Indian fund, whose land, worth, as the hon. member for Selkirk says, from $75 to $100 per acre, was *'actually sold for $5 or $6 per acre. That is the salve which is to be given to my hon. friend from Selkirk, and the salve which is to be given to the people of Selkirk is that the titles are to be confirmed. It is a petty piece of business that the
men who bought the lands in good faith, who paid the Government of Canada for them in good faith, are to be held up, with a pistol placed at their heads, and told that unless they are prepared to pay a dollar an acre more for the lands, of which my hon. friend from Selkirk says the Indians were robbed, the titles will still be held up and the matter will be taken to the Privy Council. It is a pretty small business for a Government of a great and wealthy Dominion like Canada; it is a pretty small business on the part of this Government, and one of which they ought to be ashamed. The Solicitor General says: We are not going to distinguish between the innocent and the guilty, and we will make the innocent pay a dollar an acre, just the same as the people who, we think, are guilty; we will make the poor widow, to whom my hon. friend from Edmonton referred, pay a dollar an acre in order to enable her to hold this land which her husband bought and paid for in good faith, thinking that it would afford a home.

The hon. member misrepresents what I said. I did not make any such statement as he has attributed to me. In the main, the innocent in this transaction are not those who were interested in the lands at all, but those who indirectly suffered, and who, consequently, are not called upon to pay anything.

My hon. friend is reported on page 2149 of Hansard as follows:
There is another consideration still. While the surrender may have been invalid, while in my humble judgment it was invalid legally, and while I think that that would have been the ultimate decision of the courts, this is the fact, that there were some concerned with that sale who were by no means as guilty as others, and there were some whose interest subsequently arose, and in whom there could be no guilt at all.
Hear, hear.
And yet those men are being asked to pay a dollar an acre more.
No, no, I did not say so.

Oh, yes, they are to
pay in order to get their titles, because the Registrar General has held them up. What does the Solicitor General say further. He says in effect, as does the hon. member for Selkirk, that the sale of these lands was invalid, and that the Registrar General was perfectly right in refusing to issue certificates of title because the titles were invalid. But the Solicitor General writes a letter, which is to be shown to the Regis-

trar General, and in -which, as a member of the Government, he undertakes to introduce legislation in order to confirm the title; and he expresses the view that the Registrar General ought to act upon that assurance and issue the certificates of title. Since when has the mere promise of a member of the Government to introduce legislation had the force of law in this country? If this sale was void, if no title actually passed, if the Registrar General was right in refusing to issue certificates of title, I would like to know how a letter from the Solicitor General could make those titles good, and make valid that which previously had been void. The Solicitor General says the Registrar General was entitled to take his assurance that. he would introduce a Bill. He says that the experience I have had in this Parliament during the past five or six years should convince me that this Government could pass any legislation which it undertook to introduce. That has not been my experience, not always; indeed I have heard the Solicitor General himself complain that there is another branch of this legislature which has sometimes taken a different view from the Government.

That was for the
Registrar General to decide.

My view is that lie is
indeed a presumptuous individual who would undertake to say that Parliament will simply register the decisions which the Government of the day has arrived at. It is not treating the House of Commons with proper consideration, and still less is it treating the Senate, an independent branch of this Parliament', with consideration when a member of the Government assumes that Parliament will pass any legislation which the Government thinks fit to introduce.

Will my hon. friend
read where I assume that Parliament will pass any legislation the Government may introduce?

My hon. friend said today in his speech that he had no doubt they had confidence in the statement he made that the Government would introduce legislation, and I understood him to say that even I, from my experience in Parliament during the past five or six years, would not question the ability of this Government to pass any legislation it might introduce.. Otherwise, why did my hon. friend Tefer to my experience in Par-
liament during the past five or six years? I submit that the legislation is not necessary at all. The registrar general has issued his certificate of title; he is prepared to pass the titles and to pass favourably upon them, as the Minister of the Interior said when he introduced the Bill. Therefore, the titles are absolutely good. But if the Government does not think it desirable to pass legislation confirming the titles, let it do>
the manly and square thing by the people wlm bought and paid for the lands, and simply confirm the titles instand of taking the petty course, even to please, or to give some degree of kudos, no matter how small, to my hon. friend from Selkirk, of demanding and squeezing out of those people, who, as I have said, bought the land and paid for it and are entitled to their certificates, the sum of one dollar per acre. The course of the Government has been influenced, on the one side, by the expression of a. strong feeling on the part of the people of Selkirk that it has treated the matter wrongly by delaying a settlement of the question; and, on the other hand, by a desire to in some way take the hon. member for Selkirk out of the position in which he placed himself some years ago* by asserting that this property of enormous value had been sold for a mere trifle. The Bill is not necessary because the titles are good. The registrar general has passed upon them and issued the necessary certificates. But if any legislation is thought by the Government to be necessary it ought to take the form of a Bill validating the titles and so putting an end to this question which has been before this House for so>
many years. That would be an honourable course, a course worthy of the Government of a great country like Canada. The course which is being taken to-day is a petty course which will reflect no credit upon the Government, or upon this Parliament, or upon my hon. friend the member for Selkirk.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It seems to me quite manifest, particularly from the speech of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Pugsley), that it is deemed necessary in some interests to surround this measure, which is in itself simple enough, with a great deal of matter tending to create confusion. It ought to be remembered that the matter that is being dealt with here is the settlement of a disputed question. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have approached this question on the assumption

that there was absolutely no room for dispute. They have assumed that the titles of the people were absolutely good titles. That may have been the contention of the people who have these titles. That has been the contention of hon. gentlemen on the other side. But the fact remains that there has been entertained by competent people an opinion absolutely contrary to that. I do not propose, as we are dealing with this question of settlement, to go into an investigation of what the evidence was, pro and con, as to the facts so far as the validity of the titles depended on the facts. But what we have to remember when we approach the consideration of this legislation, what we cannot afford to overlook, is that it was contended that the titles were legally invalid because the agents and trustees of the Indians at the time of the transaction had not obtained from the Indians the consent that was essential to the passing of the title. If that contention is correct, the property of the Indians was parted with illegally and surely you have at the very outset, as we have heard so much about innocent people and about this Government grasping money apparently, as hon. gentlemen consider it, for the benefit of this Government at the expense of innocent people, to remember that the contention of the Crown in this case is that the innocent Indian had been deprived of the property without his consent lawfully given. Furthermore, it was contended that the Indian, by reason of this transaction, had received less for his property than he really should have received for it. ' So, we have one clearly innocent party on whose' behalf this Government is making no pretension of its own, and making no claim for money from anybody, for itself or for its own benefit. Here, we have the certainly innocent Indian who, if the contention is sound, had been deprived of his-property through no fault o' his own and had not received adequate value for it. Not only did the Government entertain that opinion but two of thre^ judges appointed to go into the question in Manitoba entertained the same opinion and arrived at the conclusion that the titles that were so given were not valid and were not effective.
It is easy to say that all this is done at the instance or at' the instigation of this Government or of some politician, but the fact remains that these two judges came to that conclusion and I really fail to see that anything has been advanced to . support the contention that. they did not arrive at that conclusion in the honest performance of the duty that was incumbent upon them.
Under this Bill it is proposed to settle what was the contention on the one hand that these innocent Indians had been deprived of their property and had received inadequate compensation for their land. On the other hand, we had a large class of persons who had acquired these properties with the knowledge not merely of the suggestion of legal invalidity but of very serious irregularities to say nothing more of the manner in which the property had been disposed of. In that situation proceedings were taken and it was the duty of the trustee for the Indian to take proceedings to rectify the wrong done to him. It is true that, where you come to deal with the rectification of a wrong resulting from the fact that in some way or other property has passed into the hands of persons from persons not capable of giving a valid title, it may happen that innocent purchasers may be made to suffer. It may be possible, although I am not in a position to say , that some one holding this land may say that he is an innocent purchaser and that he acted in good faith. Let us assume that there are some of those; in what situation do we find ourselves then? We find ourselves in this situation, that by the, what we believe to be, illegal action and not merely the illegal action, but, if the facts put before us are proved, as apparently the evidence does prove them, the grave irregularities of those who at the time of this transaction were the trustees of the Indians, a wrong was done to the Indian. We are to-day the trustees of the Indians and even if it were true that there should be some innocent person who, because he had dealt with people who themselves had dealt in bad faith, would ultimately suffer, surely that does not relieve us of our obligation to see that the absolutely innocent Indian is protected.
While we had strong grounds for believing that the title was invalid, such a contention and belief were contested by those people immediately concerned and it was further made to appear that a large part of the community where these lands are situate would suffer if this thing were left to be dealt with by more or less protracted litigation.	In face
of that situation what did we do? Hon. gentlemen talk of extorting money from innocent people, forcing innocent people to pay money. There is nothing in this

Act that does that. We assent to a settlement for those who desire a settlement. In * view of conditions as they are to-day, we assent to a settlement that, it is true, gives less to the Indian than if the transaction had been regularly carried out he would have received. It is true we compromised his claim, we accept a reduced amount, but we extort that from nobody. Nobody is bound to come under this Act. All we say is: there is our view, there is our belief; we believe the Indian is right. On the other hand, there is the defence put up that the people acquired the property in perfectly good faith. We realize the importance, not only to the people who hold the property, but, I may say, to the community there generally, of having this matter settled once and for all. We realize too, strong as our convictions may be, that there is such a thing as uncertainty in the law. In view of these considerations, we are willing to accept from those who want their titles validated, and who feel themselves that the case against their titles is sufficiently strong to ma*e it >at least doubtful, the payment of this fnoderate sum. This Government is not trying to grab money, but when this money is paid to it as the trustee of the Indian, there will be restored to the Indian some slight part of what we are convinced he lost by reason of the administration of tne previous trustees. I do not want to raise up old questions, or to malre cnarges, but our view is that by these illegal and irregular actions of those who were acting as t^e previous trustees of the Indian, he has incurred a loss. Now we say to these people; If you will compensate, to some extent at all events, for the loss to our wards, we will, in view of the conditions, agree to accept from you a settlement upon your paying this moderate sum and we will thereupon pass legislation to validate your title and remove the doubt. Nobody is being coerced into that settlement. Any one who believes he has a good title may go on and let the courts decide it. However innocent, as I have said, any of these persons may be, the innocence of the Indian, it seems to me, is unquestionable.
It is unfortunate for those who acquired this property in perfectly good faith to find that those from whom they acquired it had no valid title, or at all events were not able to give them a clear title; but any person who in perfectly good faith acquired that property under those conditions has recourse against the persons from whom he immediately acquired it; and ultimately, 
those who will suffer are the ones who were parties to this transaction which is attacked as not only invalid, hut as attainted with such irregularities-to use the mildest word-as to make their title manifestly invalid. It may be that, in the settlement, some innocent purchaser may pay a very small part of the excess value of this property in order to clear his title; that small part will go to the absolutely innocent Indian. In any settlement of a law suit in reaching a compromise some sacrifice is usually involved on both sides, and if anybody should make a email sacrifice in this settlement it is those whose titles are being made valid rather than the Indian. If of two innocent persons one or the other must suffer because of the illegal and irregular action of a previous Government- that is the view we take of it- surely it ought to be clear that our duty is to protect that innocent party who is our ward and under our tutelage, and to leave such other innocent parties as may have been led into a loss by the illegal and irregular action of the previous Government, and by the fact that they have acquired properties from persons who had previously obtained them with knowledge of the irregularity and illegality-leave them to take their recourse against those who are. responsible.
A great deal has been said about a letter in which it was represented that it would be good for the general public, as well as for the Conservative party, that a certain thing which itself was represented as a good and a right thing to do should, be done. Well, I should hope that public opinion in this country is such that every time this Government does a thing that in itself is right and- proper, a thing that in the general interests ought to be done, to that extent it will be good for the Conservative party to do it; but because a letter of that sort was written, saying that a certain thing was a right and an honest and a proper thing for this Government t'o dp, the conclusion hon. gentlemen opposite would have had us reach was this: because, in doing this thing, which is right and honest, and to the advantage of the community that we should do, we may be doing good to the Conservative party, therefore we must not do it. That is the conclusion they would have had us reach. Every time that we do something that it is right and proper and honest that we should do, we have an abiding confidence that it will also be a good thing for the Conservative party

for us to do that. After all, when you analyse the letter which was written, that is just what it said-that it would be a good thing for the Conservative party and a good thing for the hon. member for Selkirk that this Government should do the right and proper thing and have the matter settled. The reasoning of my hon. friend from St. John is that this Government.' should at once- have said: No matter how right and good it is for the community, no matter how proper it is that this should be done, it may do some good to the Conservative1 party and to the hon.' member for Selkirk; that is a conclusive reason why we should refuse to do it. I think that sort of reasoning only needs to be stated to be treated as it deserves to be treated.
Upon the whole, the argument made in support of this amendment-I am referring now more particularly to the argument of the hon. member for St. John-has manifestly no purpose other than to create a confusion with regard to a perfectly clear and a perfectly simple matter. A good deal was said about a letter which the Solicitor General is said to have written, but which it turns out he did not write at all, and wMch was supposed to contain certain things which it does not contain. It was said that the Solicitor General had undertaken to say to the registrar general that, upon the strength of his promise that legislation should be introduced, the registrar should go on and register titles. Let us see just what the registrar says:
Sir,-I understand that a proposition has been made in regard to the titles to lands in the St. Peters Indian reserve, the proposition being that if the purchasers of the lands in that reserve will pay in cash or give a lien or charge to the Indian Department of $1.00 per acre, the Dominion Parliament will pass legislation to confirm that surrender. I understand that there are some cases in which parties are anxious now to have some of these lands released and obtain certificates of title therefor under the Manitoba Real Property Act. I may say that this proposition would be quite satisfactory to me, and so far as the latter class of cases is concerned, that is to say, where the $1 is to be paid in cash,-I would have the money paid in my office here, to be held in trust, and I would then issue a certificate of title clear of all encumbrance, to the purchaser of the lands upon which the $1 per acre has been paid In cash.
I am willing to do this to relieve the situation provided you will give me an undertaking in writing that you will introduce in the next session of Parliament of Canada, a Bill as a Government measure, to confirm the surrender in question, and will use every effort of yourself and your colleagues to have the Bill passed.
If this is satisfactory to you, please write me at once, giving the above undertaking.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant, v	(Signed) W. E. Macara,
Registrar General.
So there was absolutely no proposition of any undertaking on the part of the Solicitor General that the legislation would be passed. Whether the registrar general was wise or unwise in taking upon himself the responsibility to do what he did, upon his being assured that a measure would be introduced and every effort made to have it passed, was a matter for him to determine; and I do not see in what way that affords ground for any criticism, either of the action of the Solicitor General or of this Government. That is what the registrar general in his judgment thought proper to do. In answer to that letter a letter was written to Mr Macara, signed by the Minister of the Interior in whose department it was, as follows:
On behalf of the Government of Canada, I undertake to introduce at the next regular session of the Parliament of Canada, a Bill as a Government measure to confirm the surrender of the St. Peters Indian reserve, the validity of which is now in question on the information of this Government in the Exchequer Court.
After giving certain details, he goes on:
This Bill the Government will use every effort to have passed.
There is all that was said. And the hon. member for St. John waxes eloquent, and satirical with regard to an alleged undertaking by the Solicitor General that certain legislation would pass this House and would pass the Senate. There is not a vestige of any such undertaking in this correspondence. As I have said, whether it was wise or unwise for the registrar general to have such great faith as he ap- -parently had, that legislation so* introduced and supported by every effort of this Government would pass, is a matter for him to determine; and if there is Toom for discussion as to the wisdom of that course the hon. gentleman might discuss it with him. But when the hon. member is satirical against the Solicitor General upon the assumption that he made an undertaking which ihe never made, and when we turn to the letters to which the hon. member referred when he indulged in his satire, and find that they do not contain at all that upon which he based the satire,
I think it would he only fair and proper

for the hon. gentleman to withdraw those observations. Upon, the whole Bill and with regard to the amendment, as I said, the proposition is one of the simplest kind. It is to ratify a measure which removes a cloud resting on the title of land, as a result of the manner in which this surrender was dealt with and these properties were sold by the previous Government, and it gives to those who unfortunately hold that land an opportunity to get a clear title. Of this legislation they may avail themselves if they desire, but it leaves them absolutely free, if they feel themselves in the position claimed for them by hon. gentlemen on the other side, to go to the courts and have the matter finally adjusted. We do this in performance of our duty to the Indian who is our ward, and whom we believe -to have been illegally deprived of his property and to have lost, by the irregular manner in which it was dealt with, a substantial sum. I think no- more need be said, when one looks at the measure and -at the facts, than that this is a proposal for the settlement of a disputed question which does an injustice to nobody; which gives some compensation to the Indians and which offers to those who have acquired the property an opportunity to clear their title of the cloud left upon it by the manner in which this matter was dealt with by our predecessors.

The Minister of Justice has expressed his great sympathy with the poor innocent Indians in this -connection. Does it not occur to you, Mr. Speaker, as strange that this Government should have been in pow.er for three or four years before the wrongs of the Indians, or the injustice to purchasers, had any effect upon them? But as soon as the seat of the late Dr. Montague became at all dangerous, on account of the lack of action on the part of this Government, and on account of the action taken by my hon. friend from Selkirk, and as soon as it began to be seen that the seat of the hon. member for Selkirk was (becoming endangered, then the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General, and the Government, realize that the poor Indian is suffering as they -claim, and they immediately take action. It is as plain as anything can be that this action was taken, not in the interests of the Indian, not in the interests of the purchaser of the land, but purely and -simply in the interest of the Conservative party, and to try to make safe a couple 
of Conservative seats that were jeopardized. You can go through this correspondence that has been brought down here, and you will not find in it one single suggestion that- there was anything wrong in connection with the surrender. I am not referring to the pleadings, the vapourings during the ]%st eight years of the hon. member for Selkirk, which are practically all incorporated in those pleadings, but to the correspondence of the people interested. I say that there is not one single vestige of a suggestion that there was anything wrong in the surrender.

Would the hon. gentleman expect that there would be?
Mr. TURRIFF [DOT] I can quite understand the Solicitor General (Mr. Meigben) making the point-and it was a fair point-that the solicitor of those applying for titles naturally would not point out that there was anything wrong. I think the same can be said of the letter of Mr. Norquay, who was writing practically as one of the leading purchasers, and also with the interests of the Conservative party in the local constituencies of Selkirk and St. Andrews at stake. I would not expect him to point out that there was anything wrong. But you have here in this correspondence the resolutions of the town of Selkirk and two other municipalities, made up of Liberals and Conservatives alike, and of the boards of trade, that there was nothing wrong in connection with the surrender of these lands. Let me point out to the Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice, that if the surrender of St. Peters reserve was not legal there has not been a legal surrender of Indian lands taken in Canada. The hon. member for Selkirk stated a little while ago that this matter had not been drawn to the attention of Mr. Macara, the Registrar General, and that therefore that officer had issued the title. What a reflection upon the Registrar General of Manitoba, that because some Indian, or some white man, did not go into his office and say: This surrender is not properly taken, he issued the patents; but that as soon as somebody said that the surrender was not legally taken, he refused to issue patents. As a matter of fact, there is not the slightest doubt that Mr. Macara was prevented from issuing these patents by the late Provincial Government, and that for political purposes and nothing else, for the purpose of trying to work out something against the late Dominion Government and to enable my hon. friend from Selkirk to make a great

splutter around through that part of the country. And my hon. friend has done that. But he saw that he was going beyond his depth, and he has done his best oi late to have the matter remedied, and I give him credit for that.
If the hon. gentleman is right, and Mr. Macara held these patents back at the instance of the late Government, why did not he issue them as soon as the Government changed?
Did not the Registrar General issue these patents?
Not that I know of.
The statement is made here that the patents issued in some cases.

The Registrar General
does not issue patents, but he did not, up to this undertaking, issue titles. Now, the hon. member (Mr. Bradbury) asks: If he was prevented from issuing titles by the Roblin Government, why did he not start issuing them when the Norris Government acceded to power?
Because suit had been entered by this Government.
What difference would that make?

Suppose it did not. I do not know whether the Registrar General did not take any such action, .but I know that in the same year this reserve was surrendered, another reserve was surrendered almost as near to Winnipeg as this, and the Registrar General never raised any objection whatever, yet that surrender was taken in absolutely and exactly the same manner.
Were allegations brought in in connection with that also?
My hon. friend has been arguing all afternoon that the surrender was not properly taken because a majority of the Indians did not vote for the surrender.

That is only one reason. In all his argument, the hon. gentleman has made that point. That is only one reason, of a legal character, for determination; but other allegations are based on fraud, and these had just as much to do with the determination of the judges as had the bare legal point.

My hon. friend says that the question of fraud had just as much to
do with the decision of the judges as did the other question raised. But the judges do not say so. Two of the three judges decided that the surrender was illegal because the Indians who voted for the surrender constituted a majority of a meeting of the Indians rather than a majority of all the Indians who were entitled to vote for. the surrender. Further, the Registrar General had refused to act before the judges had come to that decision and in view of the fact that the Registrar General did not wait for the judges' report, there is not much use in the hon. Solicitor General's trying to bolster up the action by the decision of the judges. The whole trouble is that this was a political move from the beginning, and it would have continued a political move but for the fact that the constituents of the hon. member for Selkirk were getting tired of waiting for their patents. The hon. Solicitor General now says: We are charging these men an additional dollar an acre. Why, the purchasers of these lands are out the interest on their purchase money for eight years. And who are asked to pay this one dollar an acre? Is it the parties that the Government themselves say are the guilty parties? Not at all. The innocent parties are asked to pay this additional sum. If anybody is to blame in this matter, it is the late Government; that is clear. The late Government took the surrender and authorized the sale, and the sale was carried out. If the Government of the day did wrong, and if this Government felt that the payment of an additional one dollar an acre was necessary to make the matter right, then the Government ought to have paid that amount, not the people who are not guilty in any sense of the word. Nobody has ever suggested that these persons are guilty, yet they are compelled to pay, and the guilty -parties, if there are guilty parties, are lef off. For my part, I do not see that there was any guilty party.
The member for Selkirk said a few minutes ago that this land was worth $24 to $150 an acre; he spoke of one man who had gathered in a lot of it and who expected	to make a sale at	$24
an acre.	I do not doubt that. I
have seen dozens of men who expected to make sales at $50 an acre. Thousands of men throughout the West bought land in 1907 at $5 or $6 an acre, and although four or five years later that land might have sold at $50 an acre, if it were offered for



.sale to-day it is just a question whether it would bring as much as it brought in 1907. My hon. friend takes the selling price at that time and then figures the value on the highest boom in prices that ever struck the country. Is that a fair comparison? I venture the assertion that if that land were put up for sale to-day only a very small portion of it would sell for any more than it sold for then, if for as much. I know of a good many parcels of land within 20, 25 ot 30 miles of Winnipeg-as near the city as the St. Peters reserve is, and some of it nearer-which is just as good land as the St. Peters reserve, if we except possibly a little strip along the river which i3 of some value for purposes of summer residences. I know people who have tried to sell that land within the last three or four years at $6, $7 and $8 an acre, and although they have offered it for sale in a number of offices in Winnipeg they have not been able to sell a dollar's worth of it. For the hon. member to come into this House and talk about land in a reserve being worth $24 to $150 an acre-well, it is simply bosh and nothing else.

The sale that I was
referring to, in which Mr. Hyland was interested, was supposed to have taken place within the last six months. There was no boom in prices then.

It was supposed to have taken place. There have been any amount of deals in land and trades in land for apartment blocks in Winnipeg and for apartment blocks in Minneapolis in connection with which prices were put in at three times their value on both sides. I would not be surprised, therefore, to 'hear that land had been turned over at $24 an acre. If it was because something was wrong that the registrar would not registrar these titles,'it was wrong to the extent only of a dollar an acre. No matter what the land was worth, even if $150 an aq-e, it was sold for $6 an acre, and by making the price $7 an acre the surrender becomes - valid and the title good. That is exactly the argument of my hon. friend. The Minister of Justice stated just now that no one was coerced in this matter. I would like to know what coercion is. The minister says that a man who, we will say, has bought a section of 640 acres of this Indian land at the average price of $6 an acre is not coerced, although he cannot get his title unless he pays this one dollar an acre. Of course he could take suit against the 
Government and he could carry the case to the Privy Council, but if forcing him to do that is not coercion, I do not know what coercion is. It seems to me that it is the highest form of coercion.
This matter is being settled at last by punishing innocent purchasers of the land. It is being settled with the purpose of trying to help the Conservative party, and of trying to help my hon. friend and it is settled for no other reason. My hon. friend intimates that it will not help him; he is quite right. My hon. friend should have taken action earlier; he let it go too long. The case is now out of his control; the people realize what my hon. friend has had to do with this case all along. He kept it stirred up for political reasons, and when he came to the conclusion that it would not do to keep the matter going any longer, steps are taken to effect a settlement whereby the innocent purchasejs of the land are made to pay. Take the case of a man who purchased, not from the Indians, and not at the auction sale, but from some other man who purchased this land. The Minister of Justice talked about recourse, what recourse would a man in this position have? He had no idea when he purchased the lands, that there was going to be all this trouble. A large part of these lands changed hands two or three times after the sale, so that the innocent purchaser of the land has absolutely no recourse, and he can thank the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) that he is in that position.

So he does; he is going to vote for me.
Amendment of Mr. Oliver negatived, on division.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time and passed. [DOT]
At six o'clock the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.
