subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Before the Bill is read a
third time, I wish to take the opportunity of offering a measure of criticism. As a prohibitionist on principle, and an abstainer in practice, I am bound to recognize favourably any step that is taken looking toward the decrease of what I am compelled to consider the evils of the abuse of liquor, especially through the liquor traffic; and, to whatever extent this Bill meets that condition, to whatever extent it assists in the restriction of the abuse of liquor, I would be compelled to support it. At the same time, I do not feel that I would be warranted in giving it my support without pointing out how, in my judgment, it falls short of achieving that measure of influence in regard to the restriction of the evils of the liquor traffic which it should exercise.
Several provinces have undertaken to deal with this question within the limits of their jurisdiction. Amongst these provinces is that of Alberta. Alberta has adopted a law which, I believe, will come into effect on the 1st of July. That' law purports to prohibit the traffic in intoxicating liquor. It does not profess to prohibit the use of intoxicating liquor. The people of Alberta voted on that proposition, and carried it by a very large majority. I am not able to say how far the provisions of this Bill which, on their face, seem to contemplate a condition under which a province has absolutely prohibited the use of liquor, and which, apparently, were intended to meet a provincial condition which, in the case of Alberta, does not, I believe, exist, will meet the conditions in the province of Alberta.
It' appears to me that as the province has certain jurisdiction in regard to the restriction of the traffic in intoxicating liquors, and that as the Dominion has certain power and authority, it would have been well if, while the province exercised its rights, the Dominion exercised those rights which pertain to its authority. The Dominion has the right to prohibit the manufacture, importation or sale of intoxicating liquors; there is no question about that,.

and it does seem to me that, when the Dominion steps into what might be called the field of prohibition, it is not living up to its responsibilities, when, instead of exercising that authority, which undoubtedly rests in it, it assumes to supplement the authority of the provinces by means which may, or may not, be of value.
I would be inclined to believe that, in its present form, the Bill would be found to be of very limited value in supporting the prohibitory legislation that has been passed, or that is in prospect in the provinces. I am inclined to think that there is a possibility that the passage of this Bill will be accompanied 'by the assertion on the one hand that it is a measure for the forwarding of prohibition principles, and, on the other hand, that it is a measure which tends rather to protect the liquor interests from the establishment of prohibition on a Dominion-wide scale. I do not wish to criticise harshly but it does appear to me that the Bill has within it elements, whether intentionally or otherwise, that make a case for prohibition on the one hand and for the maintenance of the liquor traffic on the other hand. This would not be the case if the Bill frankly declared the exercise of the authority which unquestionably rests in the Dominion Government; that is the right and authority to prohibit ithe manufacture or importation of intoxicating liquors. That is what the Bill .most particularly does not do. Inasmuch as it does not do that, it is possible for the Government to claim on behalf of the Bill that it stands as a protection to the interests that are concerned in the manufacture and sale of intoxicants.
There is another feature of the question that I desire to draw attention to. It is a feature that, it seems to me, those who express an interest in prohibitory or temperance legislation, persistently shut their eyes to. This country has been a partner in the liquor business for many, many years. It has not only been a partner, but it has been the larger partner in the interests engaged in the manufacture of intoxicating liquor. If the figures I have received are correct, for every dollar the distiller receives for his product, the treasury [DOT] receives $2. In the partnership that exists between the country and the distiller the country has a two-thirds interest to the distiller's one-third, if you consider the question of profit. I have not been able to figure the share of the country in the 
brewery business, but there is no question that the country has an important share in the profits of the brewing industry, if it is to be called an industry. Whether it is a 50-50 share or a 60-30 share, I do not know, but it is a large and important share and we must not shut our eyes to the fact that as a country we are sharing in the profits of the brewing and distilling business. Is it a fair proposition that, having been, and being to-day in the brewery business, we introduce legislation which is supposed to supplement provincial legislation, the effect of which is to cut off the brewery business within certain provinces without' recognizing our responsibility in regard to that business? A brewery is established in a certain locality and it serves the demand of the population more or less immediately surrounding; in other words, the field of operations for the brewery is within the province in which it is located. The people of the province we will say, declare against the sale of liquor in that province. That is distinctly a blow at the breweries located in that province because a brewery cannot do business satisfactorily outside the limits of the province in which it is located. Speaking generally, it must sell within a radius of the place of manufacture and assuming that it is centrally located in the province, or approximately centrally located, if it is prohibited from selling in the province, it is practically put out of business. The Provincial Legislatures have no responsibility whatever in regard to breweries. They did not establish them, they get no revenue from them, they have nothing whatever to do with them and they are perfectly free to pass legislation that will put the breweries out of business within provincial boundaries. But I do not think that this Government of Canada is in the same position. I am prepared to say that when this Government undertakes to deal with breweries and distilleries so as to put them out of business it assumes a responsibility in regard to the investment in these enterprises that is not recognized in the terms of this Bill and I desire to draw attention to the fact that it is not the privilege of the Dominion Government and Parliament to step into this field of prohibition without assuming that measure of responsibility that properly belongs to them. The point is that when by this measure we undertake to deal with the question of prohibition of the manufacture of intoxicants we thereby render ourselves as a Dominion Parliament

responsible for the investments made in producing these intoxicants that are dependent upon their sale within the province of their manufacture.

speechtext: I would certainly say that I could not by any means see 'how this Government, Parliament, and country could relieve themselves from 'responsibility. .

speechtext: Without compensation?

subtopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subsubtopic: BILL IN AID OP PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
Without compensation, I do not see how we could. We have shared in the profits of these several businesses during half a century, or ever since we have had a country, and I cannot see how we are entitled to wipe them out of existence by legislation without recognizing the fact that investments have been made in full accord with the law and not only in accord with the law but absolutely in partnership with ourselves as being responsible for the Government of this country.
In enacting this legislation, which to some extent, steps outside of the direct responsibility of the Federal Parliament and Government, and aims at supplementing by a more or less indirect method provincial legislation, I cannot think it is fair that we'should refuse to recognize our responsibility in regard to it. I have no hesitation in taking that position, although I am a prohibitionist and an abstainer; but a dollar is a dollar, and so far as I can see, the dollar that is honestly invested in a distillery or a brewery is just as honestly invested as if it were a dollar invested in a flour mill. I am prepared to vote out the brewery and the distillery to-morrow, but I do not think that is any reason why I should demand that the man who has invested his money legitimately in the brewery or distillery should lose it. A country which desires to iniprove its condition by wiping out this manufacture should assume the financial responsibility; I cannot see that there is any other logical conclusion, and my point in regard to this legislation is that inasmuch as it brings Dominion authority to bear upon the question of provincial prohibition, to that extent the Dominion Government, in equity, has assumed the responsibility of compensation
to those enterprises that are engaged in 1 the production of intoxicating liquor and are necessarily affected by the provincial legislation that this endorses and supplements, and is presumed to make more effective.
I am bringing this matter to the attention of the House and of the country because I think it should be realized by those who are in favour of prohibition as well as by everybody else, that there is a financial side to the question, and that when we undertake to deal with it we must have regard to that financial side. As to the propriety of introducing Dominion legislation at the present moment, prohibiting the manufacture, sale, and importation of intoxicating liquor as a beverage, in my humble judgment there could not be any question as to>
its propriety, as to its possibilities, or as to its timeliness. It is true that in a Confederation, such as Canada is, there are difficulties in the way that would not exist if we were not a Confederation, but my judgment is-I am only giving this personally, I do not wish to speak for anybody else-especially in view of the very strong expression of opinion that has been given by those provinces where public opinion on the question has recently been tested, my belief is that public opinion in this Dominion is ripe for that legislation, and that the legislation is called for by the conditions existing at the present time.
There may have been times in the history of civilization when the argument was held, and possibly believed, that the liquor traffic was of benefit as a producer of national revenue. I do not think that belief is seriously held at the present time by any one. I think it is conceded now- and the example of other countries is evidence to the point-that the expenditure on intoxicating liquors is an unwise and an improvident. expenditure, that it tends to the impoverishment of the country, and is not a desirable source of revenue; that this or any other country would be far ahead financially if it were possible to wipe out at a stroke expenditure on intoxicating liquors and raise our revenue by some other means. There can be no doubt that the loss of energy and the misdirection of effort that results from an undue consumption of intoxicants is a greater burden for a country to carry, and a greater detriment to its well-being than the more direct expenditure on the purchase of liquor, and that direct expenditure on the purchase of liquor is so stupendously greater than the small

amount of revenue derived from it by the State, that there can be no question that if it were possible to wipe out the vast expenditure on liquor, the country would be tremendously advantaged, and the treasury correspondingly better off. I do not wish to present my arguments as condemning the Government; I do not wish to be understood as making a partisan argument in any way; but in view of the financial and other conditions that have arisen because of the war, and in view of the public feeling that exists-and the people are realizing more and more every day the tremendously increased burdens they will have to carry by reason of the war-I am satisfied that this is a time when the people of Canada would accept, in place of this measure, legislation simply declaring that the manufacture, importation and sale of intoxicating liquors for beverage purposes is prohibited throughout the Dominion.

speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me that, save in so far as he made some suggestion of obligation on the part of this Dominion, arising out of this legislation to compensate the manufacturers-and as to that I shall say a word in a moment-his address was to the principle of this measure, and would have perhaps been more in order upon the second reading. I do not propose to join in a discussion of that principle.
I would simply like to point out what the principle of this measure is. The underlying principle of this measure is to be found in the belief that the most important feature about legislation of this sort is that it should have effective enforcement, and that the best guarantee of enforcement of laws of this kind is that they should have the assent, as nearly as possible of the whole of the community called upon to submit to them. Starting with that principle, it seemed to us-and I think I may fairly say it seemed to this House as it has adopted the principle of the Bill, and moreover adopted the amendment of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) to the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens)-and accepting what the hon. gentleman has pointed out, and which had been pointed out many times before, that we have evidence that the different provinces desire prohibition within their limits, it seemed to us that the best method for this Parliament to exercise its powers was to exercise them in aid-	-
ing that -which each particular province might deem to be best for itself upon this subject of prohibition. The hon. gentleman said that we might have legislation in general terms, and he thought it would have been better to prohibit absolutely the importation, manufacture and sale of liquor. I want to be quite fair; I do not dispute, and have not disputed, that there is power in this Parliament to do that; but the view I have expressed, and the view intended to be carried out by this Bill, is that, if there be that power, it is not the best means to prohibition legislation that will he effectively enforced. The present measure does not propose to impose on any province a larger measure of prohibition than it chooses to enact for itself, but it does propose to protect, and I venture to say that it will effectively protect, any province to the full extent of the prohibition which it desires to enact for itself. It will protect that province in the due carrying out of its enactments and against being interfered with in so doing by the bringing of liquor into that province from outside provinces. To that extent, it deals with the importation. It furthermore deals with the importation so far as it prohibits the importation from foreign countries of liquor into a province which has enacted a prohibitory law, but it only prohibits that importation to the extent that the province by its legislation has evinced a desire for prohibition. It only prohibits the importation of liqjior into the province to be used therein in violation of the law of that province. If a province is satisfied to prohibit the traffic and does not object to the use of liquor within its limits, this law will prohibit the sending in of liquor for the purpose of being trafficked in. If the province thinks that what it want's to prevent is the use of liquor and so enacts, then automatically under this law it will be an offence to send liquor in for a use which the province has prohibited. So it leaves to the provinces to say what prohibition they want, leaves eadh community to determine how drastic a law is desired; but whatever law the province may so enact, this legislation will prevent it being interfered with from outside.
Now, if all the provinces desire prohibition to the fullest extent that they may have it, each one of them in turn as it adopts it, will be protected from the effectiveness of t'he law being interfered

with by people sending in liquor from outside. The hon.. gentleman asked:	Why
don't you prohibit at one stroke the manufacture, importation and sale? We do not do this because if we did we should be imposing it upon provinces which by their legislation have shown that they do not want the full measure of prohibition, and so we should make a law that, so far as these provinces are concerned, would not be in accordance with the spirit of the people who are subjected to it. If it be true that all the people of the province want the fullest measure of prohibition, they can give it to themselves, each one within its own limits, and this legislation will protect each from outside interference.
The provinces can protect their respective people from the evils that follow from the use of liquor by dealing with the use of liquor. They can deal with the sale of liquor, each within its own boundaries. I have said, and I venture to repeat, that ,r they have a measure, at all events, of power to prohibit the manufacture. No province, so far as I know, has prohibited the use of liquor. Because the provinces have not prohibited the use of liquor, this Act will not prevent the sending in of liquor for beverage use. If the provinces say that they want the use of liqiior prohibited, this Act will protect them in that; if they say they do not want it sold, this Act will prevent liquor being sent into the province to be sold. When a province has exercised its full powers in that regard, all that will be left would be the fact that liquor was being manufactured within the province. Their law will protect their own people against its consumption, if they desire to enact a law to that effect. As I say, they have in a measure at least the power to prohibit the manufacture. When they have reached that stage, it' will be for us to consider whether it is necessary for Parliament to enact any further legislation, or whether the enactments of the provinces have not produced-are not effective to produce-the full desired result.
I venture to say there is a measure at least' within which the provinces have the power to prohibit the manufacture. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) has given us an exact instance of the case where, I am satisfied, there can be no doubt of the power of the provinces to prohibit the manufacture. He has done that in the branch of his case, in which he seems to have been speaking in the interests of the manufacturer of beer. He suggested that this Bill might be open to the suggestion
that, whether intentionally or not, it could be said to operate in the interests of prohibition on the one side, and in the interests of the liquor traffic on the other. Does not it occur to him that his speech can be characterized in the same way-as being in the interest of prohibition to some extent, and in the interest of the beer manufacturers from another point of view? The hon. gentleman finds fault because we have not absolutely suppressed beer, yet goes on to complain, though we have not done that, that we have not provided compensation to the manufacturer for what we have done, which does not touch his right to manufacture. But in his endeavour to create a situation in which there would be a moral obligation upon this Government to compensate the brewers, he has given us an instance of the prevention of manufacture that would be purely a provincial matter. He says that, as a rule, the sale of a brewer is confined practically within his own province. That makes the brewery a purely provincial or local concern; it is not doing business outside; it is manufacturing inside and selling inside. The provinces alone, without any aid or assistance from our Act, by prohibiting the sale, as the hon. member points out, destroy the market of that brewer, and the hon. gentleman's suggestion is that this Parliament, with whom he has found fault for not prohibiting that manufacture as a Parliament, should step in and compensate that brewer for the consequences of' that which the province alone did.
I rather desire to emphasize the fact that the hon. gentleman has furnished me with one very clear instance of a case where the power to prohibit manufacture would be in the hands of the province and no province that I know, even with regard to brewers of that kind, has thought proper to exercise its power to prohibit manufacture. They do prohibit the sale, and if there be no sale outside the province 1 presume that, in the exercise of a power belonging to them, they have destroyed the business. The hon. gentleman says that we ought to compensate a brewer whom in tne same breath he describes as our partners. He says this Government was a partner for two-thirds in the brewery. When the province destroyed the market of the brewery it injured for one-third the brewer and for two-thirds this Government, if the hon. gentleman's position is correct. Because the province has chosen to suppress what the hon. gentleman describes as the partnership business of

the Government and a brewer and this Government is bearing two-thirds of the loss, the hon. gentleman says this Government ought to pay the other third which the brewer suffers. This seems to me the clearest case of non sequitur that I have come across in a very long time. The case is put as one where the exercise of provincial authority causes loss to this Government and to a brewer, and it is stated that this Government should compensate the brewer. It is to be pointed out that in that particular case this Act does not affect the transaction in the slightest degree, because the hon. member's hypothesis is that this is a brewery in a province which sells its entire product within that province and this Act affects nothing but the sending of liquor out of one province into another. How this legislation can be said in the remotest degree to hit that brewer passes my comprehension. If it has any effect at all it produces for him this amount of consolation, at all events: if his province has prevented people buying his beer within that province, this legislation will prevent his competitor outside of the province sending beer in for the purpose of being sold under his nose. That is the one respect in which it affects my hon. friend's hypothetical brewer, so that I must confess that . I can see no connection between this legislation and compensation to a brewer who may be injuriously affected. If the day comes when it shall be necessary for this Parliament to prohibit the manufacture of liquor the question will arise-which I fully recognize to be a question deserving of careful consideration- whether compensation should be extended to those who may suffer by the legislation enacted by this Parliament, and if compensation should be extended, what the measure of that compensation should be.
I hope I have made it clear that this legislation in no manner affects the supposed case that has been put before us and that the loss of that supposed ibrewer, which the hon. gentleman points out as shared by this Government, is a loss resulting exclusively from an exercise by the provincial legislature of its powers.
It has- been made a serious matter of reproach that this Government has been, as the hon. gentleman describes it, a partner in the business of the manufacture of liquor. It seems to me a rather peculiar suggestion that by some method or other this Parliament and past Parliaments are
[Mr. Dolierty.J
open to reproach because they have authorized taxation on the manufacture of liquor. That may not be as good as prohibition, from the point of view of people who want to discourage the consumption of liquor, but surely putting heavy taxation on this manufacture is legislating to discourage the -consumption. To describe the taxing Government as a partner in the business does not, it seems to me, justify the suggestion that there is any responsibility upon the Government for the existence of the manufacture. Would it be suggested that if we took that taxation off there would be less manufacture of liquor? So far as it does operate to affect the manufacture or consumption of liquor it would seem to me fairly clear that it* must operate to discourage that manufacture and consumption. That, however, I say merely in passing. I do not tihnk that that method of putting it was intended to 'have or did have a material bearing on the argument of the hen. gentleman as he made it. So far as he suggested compensation, it was in the hypothetical case that I have- mentioned, and I hope I have made it clear that in that case, whatever might be the position in regard to any other case, it is impossible, to attribute the loss of that supposed brewer to any action of this Parliament and to this legislation that I have proposed in particular

speechtext:
Just a word, Mr. Speaker, in reply to some of the remarks that have fallen from the lips of the Minister of Justice. I think my hon. friend realizes the weak spot in this Bill as a prohibitory law in regard to the sale of intoxicating liquor. I think he must realize also that the Bill as framed, entitled an Act in aid of Provincial Legislation prohibiting or restricting the sale or use of Intoxicating Liquors, falls far short of being what one might call an effective aid. The weak spot in the proposal, -as pointed out by the -hon. member for Edmonton, is that the Bill does not seek to prohibit the manufacture of intoxicating liquors within provinces which have adopted laws prohibiting the sale of intoxicating liquors. I think every one recognizes that so long as you permit beer, whisky and other liquors to be manufactured at the various centres of population in the provinces of Canada which have adopted prohibitory liquor laws, a large portion of the output will be consumed in those provinces, no matter how stringent may be the enforcement of the provincial law. The

temperance people recognize that, from one end of the country to the other. The Minister of Justice has on more than one occasion in this House maintained that his purpose in this Bill is to go just as far as the Provincial Legislatures themselves will go. That at first glance would seem to be pretty fair ground to stand upon, but we must take into consideration the fact that the Provincial Legislatures, whether rightly or wrongly, believe that they have no power effectually to prohibit the manufacture of intoxicating liquor, and that is the reason why their legislation does not go that far. When this Bill was in committee, I brought this matter up, and after listening to the speech of the Minister of Justice and giving consideration to the attitude which he then took in regard to the question of manufacture, I examined the position taken by the Legislature of the province of Ontario upon the question of manufacture within that province and the right of the Provincial Legislature to prohibit manufacture.
I find that in the month of March, 1912, a resolution was adopted in the Legislature of Ontario. That resolution was moved by Sir James Whitney, then Prime Minister of Ontario, seconded by Mr. Foy, then Attorney General of Ontario, and it was in this language:	*
That this House recognizes the duty cast upon it to minimize as far as possible the evil effect of the drink habit by wise restrictions upon the traffic in intoxicating liquors.	,
That this House also recognizes that having regard to the decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council as to the respective jurisdictions of the Dominion and of the provinces, it is impossible for the people of the province, through its legislation, to abolish or control the manufacture within, or the importation into the province of intoxicating liquors.
That is the considered judgment of the Legislature of Ontario; and in the Bill now pending before that Legislature there is no clause seeking to prohibit the manufacture of intoxicating liquors within that' province, simply because that Legislature believes it has not that power. If it had the power, I think we may fairly assume the Legislature of Ontario would enact that legislation. Now, if the Minister of Justice seriously seeks to aid in the enforcement of this law when it is passed in Ontario, or in any other province, surely he will favourably consider a clause which, when this Bill was in committee, I intimated, might be moved as an amendment when the Bill came to the House; that is a clause simply providing that in any province which has adopted a prohibitory liquor law no
license should be issued to a brewer, a distiller, or maltster under the Inland Revenue Act. To my mind that would give effectual aid to the provincial legislation now proposed in Ontario, and to similar legislation in any of the other provinces of Canada. It cannot be said that a brewer or distiller has any vested right in his brewery or distillery. It has been held that where a system of license exists no vested right exists. In asking the minister to consider such a proposal,. I may tell him that since I brought the matter up I have been informed that reputable men engaged in the liquor business heretofore, men in the hotel busi-' ness, men in the liquor store business, have expressed themselves openly to the effect that they want to see this measure made effective; they want to see the
9 p.m. manufacture stopped in the provinces which pass prohibitory liquor law's, while the provincial Act is in force. They want to see the matter fairly and thoroughly tried out. The Bill in the Ontario Provincial Legislature hits the hotel keeper and the liquor store keeper very severely financially; but these men are willing to see the matter tried out, and many of them have asked that, so far as possible, prohibition be made absolute. The way to make it absolute is to stop it at the spout, to stop the manufacture in the province while the provincial law is in force. As I intimated in the committee, I propose now to move an amendment as a substitute for section 2. Section 2 is better than no clause at all. It provides that a distiller or'brewer who three times breaks the law shall lose his license. My proposal will be that a brewer or distiller shall not get a license in a province that has adopted a prohibitory liquor law. I therefore beg to move as an amendment:
That Bill 66 be not read a third time, but that the said Bill be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House with instructions to amend the same by striking out section 2 thereof, and substituting therefor the following :
" No license shall hereafter be granted or renewed, under the provisions of the Inland Revenue Act, to any person to enable such person to carry on business as a distiller, brewer or maltster in any province wherein a Provincial Act is in force prohibiting the sale of intoxicating liquor."

shall not go over again the reasons which at that time I gave as seeming to.me to justify the rejection of the amendment. I do not know that there is anything to be gained by repeating it, but the hon. gentleman proposes that we should do something not merely to make effective provincial legislation, but to enact, on our own responsibility, prohibition of something that the provinces have not, in whatever measure they may have power to do it, thought proper to prohibit. The hon. gentleman says that the reason why they have not done so is because they think they cannot. Of course, I cannot undertake to constitute myself a judge as to what the motives of the Provincial Legislatures are in refusing to so enact; hut it does not seem to me that it is consistent with the principle of a measure that proposes to surround effective legislation by the provinces with safeguards against outside interference, that we should be asked to interject a substantial provision oif our own in the exercise of such power as the Dominion may have to deal with the subject of the ' manufacture of liquor in the provinces.

It appears clearly now that this is not a Government measure, that it is a non-partisan proposal which is before the House, and for that reason I wish to offer another amendment which I hope will be accepted by members on both sides of the HousA When the Bill was introduced, and discussed in committee a few days ago, attention was drawn to the advisability of having some provision for the enforcement of the law. It was pointed out that this is a peculiar measure in this respect, that every offence against that Act must be committed outside the province which has introduced prohibition; that is to say, that every offence, under this Bill, will be committed outside of the prohibition area and in some other province. The difficulties of enforcing the law by municipalities at a distance are so great that I think they will be recognized by everybody. I have drawn the matter to the attention of the 'Minister of Justice, and I have no doubt that he will be willing to accept the proposal I am about to make, which is not in the same language as the proposal which was substituted the other day. The proposal that was made the other day was objected to by the minister on the ground that it threw upon the Minister of Justice the responsibility of prosecuting cases within the province affected. That is not intended in this proposal. What is intended is that when an offence is committed outside the boundaries of a province which has enacted prohibitory legislation, the Department of Justice will take charge of the prosecution. I submit that that is a
reasonable proposal, and one which I think will be agreed to by the Minister of Justice, and by hon. members on both sides of the House. This Bill is not the kind of measure which the temperance people are asking for; it does- not satisfy the temperance people because it does not prohibit the manufacture -and sale of intoxicating liquor. At the same time, we all recognize that it is a step in the right direction, and, as it has been agreed to by both sides of the House, it is our duty to make it as effective ^s possible in the direction of stopping the liquor trade throughout the country. I move:
That this Bill be not now read a third time, but that It be referred to the Committee of the Whole House with instructions to add as clause 8 thereof, the following:
When it is brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice that an offence against any of the provisions of this Act has been committed outside the boundaries of any province which has enacted legislation prohibiting or restricting the sale of intoxicating liquor, he may, if the evidence put before him be in his judgment sufficient, take such steps as may be deemed necessary to prosecute any person charged with such offence.

Mr. DOHERTY": Mr. Speaker, before the motion passes, I would like to make one observation; it is in connection with much that has been said in regard to enforcement. I want to say that I have had made to me, and rather pressed upon me, the suggestion that we should insert in the Bill a provision making the fines and penalties payable to the municipality or province, or to such person or persons as may aid in the enforcement of the Act. The sugges-
	.
tion, I think, is an excellent one, but I find that there is provision in the Criminal Code whereby such penalties may be, by Order in Council, made payable to the provincial or municipal authorities or to the person or persons aiding in the enforcement of the law. It seems to me better that we should leave it to be dealt with in that way because in that way we shall be able to make provision to suit conditions that may vary in different places and at different times.
