speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The amount expended out of
this vote in 1914-15 was $549,288.75. The amount expended this year up to January 31 is $348,287.87, and to March 3 this year, $405,690.94. There is an increase tn the vote this year of $30,000, chiefly for three reasons: first, work in connection with bovine tuberculosis; second, new lines of

work; and third, preparedness. Bovine tuberculosis is now dealt with in a new manner under regulations put in force on May 14. These regulations provide for federal assistance in controlling and eradicating bovine tuberculosis from dairy herds which supply milk to cities and towns, and whose owners apply for assistance and comply with the necessary conditions The conditions are that the municipalities must provide a sanitary inspector, who must enforce satisfactory regulations with regard to sanitation. The department tests all cattle in the dairy herds free of charge, and provision is made for the slaughter of and compensation for tubercular animals. Although, as soon as this order came into force, all medical officers throughout Canada were notified, only one city, Saskatchewan, is receiving assistance at the present time. A few others have applied for it, but so far they have not made the necessary improvements to justify the department to take action. Some inquiries have recently been received, and it is quite possible that some cities may be added in the near future. The number of cattle tested in Saskatchewan dairy herds was 2,664, 80 of which were found to be tubercular. These were slaughtered, and the department paid in compensation therefor, $1,859.98, or about $25 a piece.

When the minister's Estimates were up on a previous occasion, I asked whether it was the intention of the Government, in the event of another outbreak of hog cholera, to adopt the same measures as in the past, or to use the serum treatment, which I understand the department has been experimenting with more or less? Is the serum treatment giving satisfactory results? If it is, I am sure the farmers throughout the country would be glad to have an announcement from the Government that this new treatment was to be resorted to, and it would also mean a large saving to the treasury.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Serum is now being used, and with very satisfactory results. It is the intention of the department to use that treatment in the case of hog cholera.
Is bovine tuberculosis as prevalent as in the past, or is it disappearing to any extent?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is still prevalent in
Canada, but not to any greater extent than in any other country.

I was glad to hear the minister say that the department have adopted the policy of partially compensating the farmer for diseased cattle that are destroyed, and that the animals are tested free of charge. In our section of the country, however, $20 or $25 would not buy anything better than a ten-day old calf, if it belonged to a good dairy herd, and I am afraid that before the department will get the farmers to have their herds tested, they will have to pay a larger amount of money for the animals that are slaughtered.
I know of no city that insists on herds being tested before their milk is allowed to be shipped into town; in fact, quite the opposite, so far as I know, and I know something about the milk that is going into most of the cities in western Ontario. Unless the department pays a very much larger sum as compensation for destroyed animals, the farmers will hide in every possible way the fact of there being tuberculosis in their herds. Personally, I have no exact knowledge as to the extent to which tuberculosis exists, but I believe there is a great deal of it among The herds in Ontario. Our Ontario cattle are worth very much more than what the minister mentioned as being paid in Saskatoon. At a sale in our section the other day the lowest cow went for $94, and the highest for $114; those were dairy cows; when it comes to thoroughbred cattle a great many of the farmers around us have thoroughbreds running from $200 to $400. If only $20 is paid for a thoroughbred Durham or Holstein that is destroyed, I am afraid the farmers would not say much about the animals having tuberculosis, even if they knew the. disease existed in their herds.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The basis upon which
compensation is awarded is laid down in these regulations relating to tuberculosis. I understand that there is a considerable salvage in an animal that is killed for tuberculosis. In the first place, the hide is in all cases just as good as the hide of any other cow.
Worth $7 or $8.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A considerable portion
of the meat is also quite fit for food; there is considerable salvage in that respect. The compensation that is paid for all cows slaughtered under these regulations is on the following basis: one-half the appraised value of the cow, if destroyed as a case of

open tuberculosis. I suppose that means a case of tuberculosis that is apparent.

I think that means a
case where the meat is defective. Some times only a part of an animal is affected.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
One-third is paid if the
animal destroyed is a re-actor, and is destroyed at the request of the owner; that is, an animal where you get a re-action when the tuberculin test is applied. The valuation is made by the inspector, and must not exceed the actual valuation for cattle as specified in section 6 of the Animals Contagious Diseases Act.
Section 6 of the Animals Contagious Diseases Act says:
The Governor in Council may order a compensation to he paid to the owners of animals slaughtered under the provisions of this Act; and in all cases, the value of the animal for which compensation is ordered, shall he determined by the minister or hy some person appointed by him.
2.	Such compensation may be withheld in whole or in part whenever the owner or the person, in charge of the animal has, in tht>
opinion of the minister, been guilty in relation to the animal of an offence against this Act, or whenever the animal, being a foreign one, was, in his judgment, diseased at the time of entering Canada.

Would that apply to animals slaughtered in the different abattoirs throughout the country? For instance a herd of cattle is brought to an abattoir and slaughtered, and it is discovered by the Government inspectors that they had tuberculosis. Would the owners be compensated?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It does not apply to cases of that kind, but only to animals ordered to be slaughtered by the Government inspectors.

The question is raised in different parts of the country whether the line should be drawn between animals slaughtered by the Government inspectors and those slaughtered at the different abattoirs. It seems unfair that if a man had a critter, in the rural parts of the country, and it was slaughtered by the Government inspector, he should be allowed for it, and yet that if that .same man brought that critter to an abattoir, and had it slaughtered, he should receive no allowance whatever.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I presume that the distinction would be that in one case they are slaughtered to prevent the spread of disease, and so for the general 'benefit, whereas, in

the other case, the owner takes the animal to be slaughtered for food purposes, and after being slaughtered the inspector detects that it is not fit for food.

Very often the man who bring it to the abattoir is not the one who raised the animal. The argument may be advanced that this system will not prevent the distributing of disease, and that is a point the department might do well to consider. The same is true of swine. The farmers say that over $100,000 beyond what is necessary is extracted from them on account of inspection. The minister kindly answered a question in regard to the inspection being paid for by the Government. The excuse is made that it is on account of the hogs condemned after going to the abattoir that this money is taken. The report of the veterinary general shows that 1,799,000 hogs were received in the different abattoirs throughout the country. Figuring what the buyers have been charging the raisers of the hogs, they would collect from them about $179,960 for animals condemned by the department inspector. But only 4,000 hogs were condemned, and at what would be a fair price for them, that would only amount to something in the neighbourhood of $65,000. So, you see, a great injustice is being done to the producer, by the Government not taking charge of the hogs condemned and so taking out of the hands of the buyers the chance to deal unfairly with the producers.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member refers to the drovers?

I refer to the buyers, the abattoir, or the packers; it is among them. According to the figures in the Veterinary General's report, all they could have any right to take from the farmers is $65,000-that is; allowing for the hogs con-demand at the abattoirs. So, injustice is being done, and I think the department should devise some means to overcome the hardship the farmers are having in connection with this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not see how the department is going to prevent that, nor do I see in any way its responsibility for it. If I understand the hon. gentleman correctly, the drovers have the habit or practice of exacting a certain percentage from the men from whom the hogs are bought, to cover possible loss because of these hogs being discovered to be diseased when slaughtered. That seems to me a matter between the

packer or the drover and the man who raises the hogs. So far as the Government inspection is concerned, that is paid for by this Parliament; the farmer is not called upon to pay any portion of it. That is the information I gave my hon. friend in response to an inquiry he made in the House some time ago. If I understand him, the farmers throughout the country have the idea that the amount they are paying the drover is to he counted as the amount the Government charges for the inspection. But the Government charges them nothing. It seems to be a custom that has grown up between those who buy and those who sell the hogs. I do not know how that difficulty could be overcome.

On the excuse of the
inspection, they have been extracting this fee.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Who has?

The buyers. They have
even put in their advertisements that the reason they have retained that fee was the necessity for inspection. Without' the necessary publicity informing the farmers that they do not have to pay for the inspection, the men in the rural districts believe that the Government is collecting its fees for inspection through this channel. I think that should be corrected. It is not for a private member to do it, but for the minister or the department'. But if, by means of this representation, they wrong the farmers to the extent of over $100,000, I think that some course could be taken by the department' to stop that illegitimate way of dealing with this important industry. If the Government compensates for hogs killed because they have contracted tuberculosis, or other contagious disease, the Government should compensate for hogs condemned at the abattoirs and not take from the ' men who are producing healthy hogs a fee to make up for the losses caused through hogs of inferior quality. If one section of the country produces a healthy lot of hogs, why should the packers or the buyers take a portion off the price of every lot that the farmer brings in? If you are going to allow this practice to be carried on, by these people the only fair thing to do is to say to them: we will allow you, as we do under the Contagious Diseases Act, a portion of the loss, and settle it in that way. An amount could be put in the Estimates to cover such payments, and then the burden would fall equally upon
the producers in all parts of the country, and not unfairly on a few.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Veterinary Director
General informs me that the department has caused; a statement to be published in the Agricultural Gazette and in the different farmers' publications throughout the country, pointing out that the farmer is not called upon to pay anything for the cost of inspection; that that cost is borne entirely by the country, and that there is no reason why the farmers should contribute anything for that purpose. That statement has been given wide publicity through tlje publications to which I have referred. He further informs me that certain packers throughout the country used to have a statement on their letterheads to the effect that a certain amount had to be paid to them for the purpose of covering Government inspection, and that they have been compelled to take that statement off their letterheads and cease giving these false statements to the farmers throughout the country. I entirely agree with my hon. friend that every possible publicity should be given to this fact. From what the hon. member for Kent says, the abuse is evidently rather widespread. I will certainly call the attention of the officials of the department to the matter, and if they have not taken all possible steps to make these facts public in the past I will give instructions that they do so in the future.

If, as the hon. member for Kent says, only 865,000 worth of hogs were condemned last year, whereas the packers and buyers charged about $170,000 in this respect, I think that the Veterinary Directol General might take the matter up with the *slaughter-house people and intimate to them that if this overcharging continued they will get into trouble with the department. As a matter of fact I do not think that the bulk of the farmers have the impression that the charge referred to is for Government inspection. The slaughterhouse people, so far as I know, have stated that the charge is to reimburse them for *the swine that are condemned by the inspectors. That is really what it is for, and I suppose if the slaughter-house people were making a reasonable profit, their claim in this respect would be legitimate. Where they are making large profits, however, I presume the farmers, think they should make up the loss. These charges are not made in all sections of the country; ap-

parently they are confined to sections where the competition is not so keen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: After all, it is a matter of contract, is it not, between the packer and the man who sells the hogs?

Very few farmers ship direct to the packer. In our section of the country there is a packer in Ingersoll, and the farmers take their hogs direct to the packers there. I do not think they exact that charge there; they may, but I have never heard that they did. I have never taken hogs there; so I do not 'know. In some sections of the country they do not exact that charge. They started to exact it, but the farmers refused to sell to them on that basis. I do not know what publicity the department give to the question of tuberculosis. Each year when the estimates of the Department of Agriculture have been up I have urged that we would never get rid of tuberculosis among the herds until the department paid compensation as they do in cases of hog cholera, or glanders. I have always been told, however, that this would be too expensive an undertaking. I take a good deal of interest in agricultural matters, an this is the first time I have heard that indemnity is paid to farmers whose tubercular cattle have been condemned. I would suggest that this be given full publicity. Bepresentatives of the Ontario Agricultural Department who are stationed in all sections of the country should be informed of this so that they may Ibe able to give the information to people with whom they come in contact. As to its publication in the Agricultural Gazette, I do not know what publicity it would get from that source., I know that this publication comes to members of Parliament, nine out of ten of whom, I think, throw it in the waste-paper basket. I occasionally read it, or parts of it, but I do not believe the ordinary farmer ever sees it unless it is sent to him by some member of Parliament. I do not know that as a fact, but I have never seen that publication in any farmer's hands, so that what publicity it gives to the fact that indemnity is now paid for condemned tubercular cattle is more than I know. It cannot he very large, or I would have heard something about it from my friends and neighbours.

I agree with my hon. friend from North Oxford that the municipalities who should he interested in the very

liberal provision that has been made under this Act do not seem to be well enough informed. Whether it is through their lack of interest or through their neglect to read the material that has been placed in their hands, I do not know. We are told by the minister that only. one city has so far availed itself of the provisions of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Since this report was published, Begina has come under the Act.

That makes two. When we consider the large area of our country and the number of large cities and towns where milk from dairy herds is sold and distributed to the people for consumption, it does seem regrettable that the municipalities themselves, in the interests of health and of human life, should not have availed themselves of the opportunities of inspection by complying with the provisions of this Act. The member for North Oxford has suggested that a good deal of the literature that goes out from the Department of Agriculture does not get the necessary distribution or is distributed in such manner that it is not appreciated by the public. I think that too much dependence is placed on the distribution of pamphlets and literature of this kind, and too little advantage taken of the public press and agricultural papers for the dissemination of such information. For instance, in the Agricultural Committee a short time ago, we had a very valuable address which might have been circulated with great advantage through the public press. It was suggested that the information be circulated by means of advertisements in the agricultural press. But even that would not fully have served the purpose intended. I am convinced that some more aggressive, measures should be taken to stamp out tuberculosis and to prevent the use of tubercular cattle in dairy herds supplying milk for cities and towns. Wherever there are medical health officers, inspection of all such herds should be insisted upon. I would suggest that communications similar to those sent to medical health officers should be sent to the municipal councils. By a more thorough system of inspection a great deal of this communicable disease, which is doubtless spreading throughout the country, might be prevented.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My information is that every health officer in Canada and all boards of health have been supplied with this information. After all, it is a matter really for the

municipality or the board of health of the municipality to deal with. If they take it up, then the department sends its inspectors and aids them in every way. Saskatoon has been more progressive in this respect than most municipalities, and its example has been followed by Regina. These regulations only came into force in June, 1914, and it always takes time for a matter of this kind to become known and appreciated. We can only hope that, as the advantages of such inspection become more apparent, other towns and cities will avail themselves of the provisions of this Act.

I was requested to bring this matter to the attention of the department and of the country by a gentleman who for many years was veterinary director general for Canada, and who is now an honorary veterinary adviser. , I refer to Dr. McEacliren. He points out that the constantly increasing use of milk for human consumption, as well as for the feeding of small stock, is a great menace to the general health of the country. The greatest enemy of humanity is tuberculosis, and Dr. McEachren points out that in many countries the number of infected animals is often as high as 50 per cent. Happily it is very much less in Canada.
I would not like to say that.

I imagine that the discussion we have had to-night would be of interest to Dr. McEachren, because I inferred from his conversation and his correspondence that he was not aware of the progress made in the last year in respect to compensation for slaughtered animals. After all, it is only a half-way measure as compared to what we are doing in compensation for diseased horses. We are giving very much less as compensation for diseased cows, slaughtered for tuberculosis, than we are paying for horses destroyed for glanders; and I think it would be well for the department to sed if they could not do more to encourage the farmers in the stamping out of tuberculosis. As has -been pointed out by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), there is an inclination now to hide cases of tuberculosis when they occur. For instance, it is well known that a drover going through the country and buying cattle to take to Montreal, may come across an animal that is condemned and sent to the tank. The drover gets the hide and then says to the farmer: "Your animal has been condemned, and unless you refund
the money I paid you I will give information that I obtained the animal from you." Often the farmer, rather than have it known that the diseased animal was purchased from him, will pay the drover the amount he received for the animal. Not only is that an injury to the farmer, but it may injure his neighbours through the spread of the disease from 'his infected herd. I hope that the Government will make a greater effort to stamp out this disease, which is such a menace to human life.

I desire to call attention to
the Canadian trade in eggs. We are building up quite an extensive trade in eggs with Great Britain, and the industry is one of great importance not only to farmers, but to others engaged in raising hens. I am instructed that the Canadian egg is in great favour in the British market, and that our prices are from 5 cents to 10 cents a dozen higher than the price of American eggs. My attention has been called, by men of reputation in the egg business in western Canada, to the fact that large dealers are importing eggs from the United States in bond. They take them to an inland city like London, or some other city near the border, and, under the bonding privilege, re-pack them, and, where the American eggs are defective, substitute Canadian eggs. Sometimes they even exchange cases. These American eggs are then exported from that point to Great Britain, the cases marked in large letters " Packed in Canada." The result is that the British consumer is deceived in the quality of the egg he is buying, and the reputation of the Canadian egg is depreciated. Consequently, the price to the Canadian producer is lowered. This results in a great loss to those interested in the production of eggs. I submit to the minister that very drastic steps should be taken by his department to see that this practice is not continued. If this is an abuse of the bonding privilege accorded to these large firms, the privilege should be either taken away or its use should be closely watched by the department. The Canadian egg industry must not be injured by such a practice. I place this matter before the minister -in order that he may draw the attention of his officers to it and that steps may be taken to avoid this injury to an important Canadian industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My attention was called to this matter a few weeks ago by my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder). I



understand that the department had a number of representations on the subject. The eggs produced in Canada have a value, I believe, of over $23,000,000 or $24,000,000, and they are increasing. As was pointed out by the hon. member from Middlesex (Mr. Ross), the Canadian hen is supposed to be superior to her sister in the United States, and to produce a better quality of egg, and it is most undesirable that eggs of an inferior quality should be brought into Canada from the United States, packed with Canadian eggs, sent to the markets outside, and sold as Canadian eggs. If they are of an inferior quality, our eggs do not get the credit that is due to them, and their price depreciates. The Customs Department has dealt with this question, I understand, and any eggs that are brought in from the United States or from any other country, have to be branded with a mark showing where they are from. The following is an Order in Council which was passed on the 27th April, 1915, and copies of which were addressed to the collectors of customs at different ports throughout Canada. It reads:
Regulations for the marking of packages containing eggs imported into Canada or passing in transit through Canada have been made and established by Order in Council of 27th April, 1915, as follows, viz.:
1.	Every package containing eggs imported into Canada or passing in transit through Canada shall have marked thereon in plain letters the word " produce " and the name of the country whence exported directly to Canada.
2.	The brands or stencils for such marking shall be supplied by the Department of Customs, in the form approved by the Minister of Customs, and the marking of the packages containing eggs shall be done at the expense ofj the importer or shipper, under, the supervision of a customs officer.
3.	It shall be the duty of collectors of customs, at ports where imported eggs are entered for consumption or for warehouse or for exportation, to see that all packages of such articles are plainly marked as prescribed by these regulations.
4.	Packages of imported eggs entered for warehouse, if not properly marked or branded, shall be marked in such warehouse under the supervision of the customs lockers in charge, who shall see that all such packages are marked according to regulations, before they are de>-livered from warehouse.
5.	Customs officers attending the delivery of imported eggs entered for consumption in Can' ada or in attendance when the same are being
laden in transit on board vessels or cars' for exportation from Canada, shall personally supervise and enforce the marking of all packages of such eggs.
That seems to ensure that any package of eggs coming into Canada will be marked so as to show where it comes from. Some one may take the eggs out of the packages,
[M. Hazen.J
however, and mix them with other eggs that are being sent out. I understand that under the provisions of the Inland Revenue Act any person "who does so is liable to a very serious penalty. It is a criminal offence to do that sort of thing, and so there is protection in that respect. The only question is that of enforcing the law. If any person in Canada knows of anyone who has taken eggs that have Come from the United States, put them into other packages, and sent them out to the markets representing them to be Canadian eggs, and lays a complaint against the party so offending, that party is liable, under the Criminal Code, to a very severe penalty. But I think the egg dealers of Canada want to go much further than that. I think they want regulations passed for the standardization of eggs. They would have inspectors to go from place to place inspecting the eggs and standardizing them, so that they would be sold, say, as No. 1, No. 1 extra, or No. 2, according to different grades. That is what the Canadian dealers are agitating for, but to carry that out would involve a very considerable expenditure. I am told we would require a staff of inspectors all over the country, and that the expense would probably, amount to $40,000 or $50,000 a year, if a policy of that sort were adopted. Being only temporarily in charge of the department, and expecting the return of the Minister of Agriculture in a very short time, I did not feel like entering upon a movement of that sort. I felt that it should be dealt with by the hon. minister who is at the head of the department, instead of by one like myself, who does not pretend to have a very great knowledge of the subject, and who will cease within a few weeks to be the acting minister. But I made inquiry into the subject, and I know that it is one worthy of very careful consideration. The department, I think, realizes that, and will give it the	best consideration possible- A sum of $50,000 a year, when we consider the value of the eggs produced in Canada, does not seem such a large amount, and an expenditure of that kind might have the effect of further encouraging the business, and of putting it on an even better footing that it is on today. From my conversation with the officials of the department, I am satisfied that they are looking very carefully into the whole matter, and that they are alive to the importance of the question raised by my hon. friend.
Can the Acting Minister of Agriculture inform me what is the size of the letters used in stencilling the packages? I am informed that they" are very small and inconspicuous.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Deputy Minister of
Agriculture tells me that the letters are branded into the wooden packages. They are not put on with a stencil, and they are good sized letters, probably an inch or an inch and a quarter in length.
Mr. MeCOIG: I would like to draw the attention of ithe department to the fact that the producers of com in the counties of Essex and Kent are being discriminated against in the matter of freight rates. I have a statement here which will explain itself. It gives a comparison between the rates paid by the farmers who are shipping corn from Essex and Kent to the Maritime Provinces, or to other portions of the Dominion where corn is wanted for feed purposes and those paid by the American farmer. The statement is as follows:
The rate that we are charged by the Canadian railroads is 23 J cents per hundred pounds to points in the lower provinces whereas our American friends across the border are enjoying a rate on corn shipments from Detroit to the lower provinces of 12J cents per cwt. Thus a discrimination against the Canadian shipper of 11 cents per hundred pounds, which practically kills our trade.
This statement is made by some of the farmers who want to ship corn from the counties of Essex and Kent. I am also informed that in shipping corn for feed purposes during a certain period of the year a much larger rate is charged for corn shipped for seed purposes, so that the farmer desirous of shipping corn to feed cattle in the other provinces has to pay an increased price compared with the Tate charged to an American farmer who brings it say from the state of Michigan. This is a matter which I think the department should endeavour to have righted, so that the American farmer may not be in a position to bring his corn into Canada at a lower rate than that paid by the farmers of the counties of Essex and Kent.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I shall be very happy to call the attention of the seed commissioner to the matter referred to, and to ask him to take it up with the Railway Commission. I think that is all we can do in regard to it.
Mr. MeOOIG:What ithe minister says only shows how unfortunate it is that the department is represented by an Acting
Minister of Agriculture instead of by the Minister of Agriculture. This is a matter in which the Minister of Agriculture would have	interested himself if he had
been	looking after the department.
We hear complaints coming from the producers and we naturally expect that the farmers will look to the Minister of Agriculture for relief in matters of this kind.
Mr. ROBB- Do we understand rightly from the minister that it is a criminal offence to put imported goods into cases and brand end export them as Canadian prods'.
Yes; if you were to fate eggs from the United States and export them to England as Canadian eggs that wculd ne a criminal offence under Ue Criminal Code.

Any man in the trade in
Montreal, Toronto or anywhere in Canada, will tell you that in 1914, when Canada contributed 1,000,000 bags of flour as a gift to the British Empire, a large proportion of the flour was milled from United States wheat in bond, put into bags provided by this Government, branded as Canadian product and shipped to England. I wonder if the minister has ever heard of that or read of it in the trade journals.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I never did.

I wish to get from the minister some information in regard to an agricultural product in which the people of Prince Edward Island are very much interested and that is hay. Will the minister tell me if the Government have any person in Prince Edward Island representing it in the purchase of hay for the British Government or for this Government, and if so, whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I understand that some
time ago there was a considerable quantity of hay bought in Prince Edward Island for shipment across to the British Government. I do not know whether at the present time any is being- bought but I do not think so.
I understood there was.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman may
be right; I cannot tell offhand.
Could the minister give me the names of the parties who purchase the hay and the amount and price?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No doubt the hon. gentleman will remember questions of that so.-'

being put in the House which were not answered at the time on the ground that' it was not in the public interest at the present time that they should be answered. But I could not say offhand because I have not the information in my possession.

I am complaining because that is the answer that has been given to the members of this House. I find that in the provincial legislature members-have information in regard to this matter that' we cannot get here. I will read the information to the minister on this question. My hon. friend from Missisr quoi (Mr. Kay) put a question on the Order Paper in regard to the purchase of hay in the several provinces and the department gave this answer:
Mr. Hazen:	It is undesirable in the public
interest to give information on such matters at the present time.
In the Legislature at Charlottetown, Mr. Leonard Woo'd, one of the members speaking upon this subject, made the statement that Carvell Bros, of Charlottetown, acting as agents for this Government or the British Government, had purchased ha/ and that the price paid was $21.50 a ton which had been increased to $22.50. I would like to know if that information is correct.
Mr HAyEN : I would not venture to say whether it is correct or not.

I do not want incorrect information to go over the country. Then I understand that in Montreal and St. John the price paid was $24 a ton. It would be very desirable to know whether these statements are correct or not. Surely it would not be an injury to the Admiralty, or the Army, or to the British Government, for this House to know if this Government were purchasing hay for the British Government in Prince Edward Island and whether they were paying a certain price per ton for it. By no possibility could that information be of any use to the enemy. I do not see why it should be withheld. With other members of the House I have been trying to get some information in regard to horses. We have received the same answer, that it was not in the public interest to give such information, but we see that information is quite freely given in the United States. A short time ago I saw it published in the papers that the British Government had purchased some 500,000 horses in the United States at a cost of $125,000,000. Later on I saw it reported
[Mr. Hazen.I
from Washington that the allied countries had purchased 678,443 horses and mules in the United States of a value of $132,000,000. That information is given out, anybody who wants it can get it and why it should be withheld from members of this House is something I cannot understand. Surely the minister could give some better explanation than merely to say that it is not in the public interest. There is some information of importance that I could readily understand that it would not be in the public interest to give to enemy countries but I cannot see how the statement that the Government had purchased a certain quantity of hay in Prince Edward Island, and paid $21, $22 or $23 a ton for it, would be giving information to Germany and other .enemy countries that they could use to our disadvantage. To refuse each information is not to treat members of this House with proper courtesy. It is not reasonable. I would suggest to the minister the propriety of looking into this matter and giving information of this kind to members who ask for it.

(iLaprairie-Napier-ville) (Translation.) Before the vote on this item is taken, I would like to make a few remarks concerning the embargo by which the Canadian Government prohibits the exportation of hay to the United States. I would not object to the Government putting on this embargo provided they were ready to take our nice No. 2 and No. 1 hay at the same price that we can get for it in the States. Number one hay brings $28 a ton in New York and all through New England.
What strikes me more than anything else is that the Department of Agriculture buys United States hay and has it re-pressed at Montreal. The hay is imported from Michigan and would hardly find a market in New York; for the last three months the price has varied from $12 to $15 a ton. You need nothing else to understand that such hay has suffered from unfavourable weather- conditions. How comes it, Mil'. Chairman, that the department, when in need of hay, goes to the United States, pays for No. [DOT] 3 hay $18.50 and $20 for ordinary No. 2 hay f.o.b., Montreal, when the same quality sells on the United States market, even i.n New York, at $10 to $15 a ton.
At the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I stated that No. 1 hay was selling at $28 a ton in the United States; let us bring it down to an average of $27; take off the charges and the dealer is left with

$21.50 f.o.b. shipping place. I infer that the Americans know full well the value of the goods.
True it is that we have the Montreal market; but it is quite restricted. Montreal pays $21 a ton for hay No. 1. Take off the freight charges, say an average of $1.50 a ton, and you get for our fine hay only $19.50, $2 less than could be had on the American market. So, I wonder why the Government prevents the farmers of the province of Quebec from selling their good hay in the United Spates, which is the only market we have, except Montreal, where a few carloads may be sold now and then. You know as well as I do that the Department of Agriculture does not purchase everybody's hay. One must be on the so-called right side of politics to be able to sell hay to the Department of Agriculture, with the result that we are at the mercy of those who have secured contracts. So I claim, Mr. Chairman, that it would be a saving to the Department of Agriculture to pay $23 a ton at Montreal for No. 1 hay from the counties of Laprairie-Napierville, St. Johns-Iberville, Bagot, Mississquoi and all the counties along the south shore, rather than pay $20 for the cull from Michigan.
Mr. Chairman, I have much experience in that trade. I have been dealing in hay for the last twenty-one years. I have had dealings since last September with a New York man who tplls me that the' Michigan hay is worthless this year for the New York market on account of the hay having been damaged in the field by continuous ibad weather during hay time.
At the start, when the first shipments were effected from Michigan to Montreal, many tons of that hay were condemned by the inspectors and before disposing of it to local buyers in Montreal the duty had to be paid. So care was taken to have inspectors on the spot in Michigan, to examine the hay before shipping it to Montreal. The people of Quebec were not so leniently dealt with. In my remarks of the 22nd of February on the budget speech, I pointed out that a large number of small dealers had been ruined because their hay had not passed inspection and was left on their hands and they had to pay demurrage on it.
But since 1911 the Americans have seen a change of conditions. At that time, it was a crime to deal with the United States; but to-day, Canadians are prevented from selling their hay on the other side of the line; while the Government goes out and buys 25,000 tons of hay in Michigan and has it
pressed in Montreal. The Government today is not backward in dealing with the Yankees.
I urge on the minister the removal of the embargo on our No. 1 hay. Since the Government will not buy it, let them give the farmers of my district the opportunity of disposing of it on the American market.
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the committee any longer. The only purpose of my remarks is to help my constituents and the people of the south shore of Montreal who might have hay for sale.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend from Laprairie, who I know is very much interested in the hay business, I may say that the Department of Agriculture in its purchases for the British Government bought hay from no one except Canadians. All the contracts were made with Canadians, and all the contracts specified Canadian hay. We believe that all the hay that was purchased was Canadian hay.

The department is not receiving hay at Montreal from Michigan?
- Mr. HAZEN: No, certainly not.
i Mr. LANCTOT: You are receiving many carloads of hay from Michigan.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: So far as the Department of ^Agriculture is concerned, we are doing nothing of the sort. We are buying no hay from Michigan. All our contracts are with Canadians, and for Canadian hay. It may be that some hay from Michigan has been passed off as Canadian hay; I will not say that that is not the case; but in any event the quantity could not have been very large. I repeat, all contracts, without a single exception, were with Canadian firms and for ^Canadian hay, and they specified the proportion of timothy and clover there should ,be. All the hay purchased is subject to inspection. That is the information I have received, and I believe it to be correct. While it may be true that possibly some of these contractors have passed off hay from the United States as Canadian hay, the department does not believe that it has been done to any considerable extent.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I must tell the minister that Michigan hay has been coming for a long time to Montreal, and it comes in bond, which shows that it is for export. .
The minister has thrown doubt on the story that hay was imported from Michigan. Let me tell him that after the Easter recess I will furnish him with the proof

that Montreal dealers ply that trade on a large scale and have been doing so for a long period. I shall moreover give him the number of carloads that were shipped to the Montreal docks every week billed to the Government. He will find that many more were shipped than he imagines.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I cannot follow my hon.
friend as closely as I should like, but I understood him to make the assertion that inspectors were sent by the Canadian Government to Michigan to inspect hay there. The Deputy Minister of Agriculture tells me that as far as he knows there is no foundation for that statement at all, and my hon. friend has been misinformed with regard to it. In view of what my hon. friend has said I shall certainly see Mr. Ruddick, the Live Stock Commissioner, tomorrow morning, and get him to ascertain if there is any foundation for the statement or not. I do not question my hon. friend's bona fides in making the statement to the House, but I am very strongly impressed with the idea that he has been imposed upon, and has received information which is not correct.
Mr. LANiOTOT: (Translation.) Mr. Chairman, at the outset of his remarks, the minister stated that no hay was imported from Michigan, and that the department had made contracts only with Canadian dealers. Yet, he added, it might be that Canadian dealers had bought hay in Michigan. In any ease, let me tell the minister that a large quantity of hay conies in by the Soo line at a special rate of $5 a ton for Montreal. I must state that I have a better knowledge of this question than the minister may suppose.

Can the minister give
me the information now with regard to hay purchased in Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have already told my hon. friend that I cannot give him the information.
What public interests would suffer by my being given that information?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is a matter of public policy for the Government, and I do not think my hon. friend ought to press his question further.
The matter is freely discussed in the legislature of our province.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They may discuss it on very incorrect information.

That is exactly why I want correct information. It is almost ludicrous to say that some public interests would suffer, or that Germany would be advantaged by my being informed how many tons of hay were purchased in Prince Edward Island, and how much was paid for it. That is carrying the privilege of refusing to answer questions to the limit.

Does the minister think it fair that the farmers of my locality should be prevented from shipping their No. 1 hay to the United States when the Department of Agriculture does not purchase any No, 1 hay? If the department was buying No. 1 hay I would not say a word, but as they are not, why should not the embargo be removed and our farmers be allowed to ship their No. 1 to the United States,,where they could get the best price for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hay is required for Great Britain or our Allies for the purpose of carrying on the war, as it is represented to be, it is a perfectly fair and proper thing for this department to put an embargo on hay. The very best hay that can be purchased in Canada is being bought for this purpose.
Does the minister think it fair that our farmers should only get for their No. 1 hay what the' department is paying for culls from Michigan?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would not think that
fair; but we are not buying any culls from Michigan.

I say you are, and I
say it without fear of contradiction. I know what I. am talking about. In my speech on the Budget on February 22 last, 1 stated that some hay which I had offered to the department was refused by the inspector, and then stored with the Baillar-geon Company on Ontario street, Montreal. The hay was afterwards sold to a Tory, and then passed the Government inspector.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A great deal.

It has been suggested
that Russia might not have as great objection to allowing exports to Canada one of the Allies, as she would have in the case of neutral countries, and I am told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that that view is being urged on the Russian Government at the present moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has been arranged for.

Yes, for the United
States, but it had not been arranged for Canada two or three days ago, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce informed me a day or so ago that the Russian Government was allowing the export of a certain quantity to the United States, and that he was pressing the Russian Government to allow the rennet to be exported direct to Canada. Under the circumstances, Canada might well expect to receive preferential treatment over neutral countries. Has any progress been made in the matter in the last two or three days?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand that the matter has been practically arranged. It is, of course, a very important question, as rennet is a staple in the manufacture of cheese. The rennet that is used in our cheese factories nearly all comes from the United States, and they get it from Russia and Denmark. Owing to arrangements that have been made within the last day or two, the officials of the department feel sure that we shall have no difficulty in getting all we want from the United States. The deputy minister tells me he received information to that effect from Mr. Ruddick on Saturday.	[DOT]

A question of very great importance in our part, of the country is horses. If it is not disclosing State secrets, would the minister tell me whether an embargo will be placed on Canadian horses going into the United States this year? As the hon. gentleman knows, we have a large surplus of horses, and we should like to get rid of a lot of them. We have been able to send some through to Michigan and
other states. American buyers are coming in there now, and paying larger prices than our farmers can get from Montreal or Toronto, buyers, and I feel sure that if our farmers knew there would be a market for their horses during the present year, a lot more horses would be bred this season. It is extremely important that the farmers should be given every encouragement in horse raising. I should like to have the assurance of the minister that there will be no embargo this year on Canadian horses going into the United States.

The placing of an embargo on any article going out of Canada is a matter for the Customs Department to deal with. There is no embargo on horses at the present time, and I do not think there is any intention of placing an embargo on them this- year, unless of course we get further instructions from the British Government,.
The embargo has been taken off?
Yes.

I should like the Government to consider carefully the argument advanced by the hon. member for La-prairie. He is in the hay business and knows what he is talking about. If it is true, as he says, that there are large quantities of No. 1 and No. 2 hay throughout the country, would it not be well for the Government to look into the matter, especially as we are on the eve of a new crop, and if the Government does not want the hay, raise the embargo and let the farmers sell it in the United States. We made a little mistake on .the horse business, and as a result horses were piling up until we did not know what to do with them. But the embargo, has been raised, and now there is a market The farmers of this country had to feed these horses when hay and oats were very expensive. It cost them a lot of money to hold these horses in stock for the British Empire, and one day we woke up to find that they were not wanted for the British Empire and so they sent them to the United States. Do not make the same mistake with regard to hay. If the hay is not wanted in Canada, then raise the embargo and let it go to the market where it is wanted.

If, as stated by an hon. member this evening, you are not paying the same price for No. 1 hay as the owners of it could get elsewhere, you are not fair

to those owners. You are paying the same price for every other class of goods that is paid in the open market-where there is open competition, you have to pay. If you put on an embargo, and so stop competition, you say, in effect, that might is right. But, might is not always right, and it is not right to take the farmer's hay at a lower price than he can get for it in another market. I do not know anything as to the facts my.self, but the hon. gentleman who spoke apparently deals in hay and ought to know what he is talking about. I think the minister should take this matter into his serious consideration; I do not believe that he would endorse anything of the kind complained of. I would recommend that the department give greater publicity to the fact that they are paying a certain percentage of the loss upon cattle.that are slaughtered under Government inspection because they are affected with tuberculosis. I doubt that there are many farmers in this country who are aware of it. 'The acting minister says that the regulations came in 1914; but if I am not mistaken, I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell) himself, the last time these Estimate? were under discussion as to that very point, and he told me that the Government could not afford to pay an indemnity in the case of bovine tuberculosis. I would certainly suggest that literature on that subject be sent to the resident representatives of the provincial Department of Agriculture, so that thiy could inform any farmers or veterinary surgeons throughout the country exactly what these regulations are.
Mr. H. BOULAY': (Translation.) I notice that we are voting large sums towards maintaining the health of animals. I deem it part of my duty to inquire from the hon. gentleman as to how these moneys are being spent. In that part of the province of Quebec which I have the honour to represent, I do not think the people are aware, as a rule, that the Dominion Government is concerned with the health of animals. Might I inquire from the minister who are the officers appointed by the Government to look after these matters in the province of Quebec, and where do they reside?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have here a list of them. These are largely veterinary inspectors, and the most of them are employed in the western provinces where, of course, the greater production of cattle takes place. I see that we have a veterinary inspector at St. Johns, Quebec, Mr. J. O. Guy, salary

$1,500; Mr. J. Halle, at Point Levis-he is not a veterinary inspector; Mr. Beaudry, in Sherbrooke; Dr. Gauvin, in Quebec, also Mr. Couture, in Quebec; Mr. Samson, who is employed at Levis; Mr. Oromwell, at Coaticook; Mr. Deers, at Montreal; Mr. Devlin, at St. John.

1 wish to refer again to this question of hay. This was discussed some weeks ago, and I took part in that discussion. But, inasmuch as my hon. friend from Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Lanctot) has referred to the matter, I desire to add a word. I have saved some hay myself, no great quantity, but my experience is sufficient to illustrate the point that is raised_here to-night. Early in the winter I had an offer of $13 a ton, and would not sell. Inside of the last three days I had an offer for my hay of $16 a ton, on condition that the embargo is raised between now and the first of June.
Mr. 'HAZEN: Is that highland or marsh hay?
Marsh hay, dyked land.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: English -marsh?

Yes. My case is an illustration of hundreds of others; there are many who might dispose of their hay in the same way if the embargo were removed. If the Imperial Government requires this hay for the keep of their horses during the war, I do not think there is a farmer who would not be quite willing to keep his hay for that purpose. It is somewhat unfair to have him keep his hay on hand if it is not needed for the use of the Empire, when the market is calling for same. With the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) I would ask the minister to consider carefully whether or not this embargo could be raised and so give the farmers an opportunity to sell their hay at the highest price.

I have a matter to bring to the attention of the Acting Minister of Agriculture that has affected the county I have the honour to represent. It has reference to horses. A gentleman came to me during the period when horses were being purchased and he asked me about a man named Robinson, of Toronto, who was supposed to be buying horses for Government. I had not heard anything about him, so I rang up Sir Adam Beck at London. He acknowledged that'the purchase of horses east of Winnipeg was entirely under his

control. I asked him to give me the place of residence and street address of this Mr. Robinson, but h,e did not know it, although I understood that Mr. Robinson was his appointee. My friend, a reputable farmer in the neighbourhood, sitting beside me in the office, was at a loss to know how to get the information. I wired to Ottawa, and in the course of two hours I got an answer to the effect that if I consulted Sir Adam Beck at London he would give me the necessary information. What was a representative of the people to do in a case like that? There was nothing to do but to feel that one was not representing the people. I put this forward in' connection with another circumstance. I was told that General Benson had charge of the purchase of horses for the British army. Upon endeavouring to see him I was referred to Colonel Benson, a brother, I think, of General Benson. He told me that the General was in Mont- -real, and that if I addressed a letter in his care it would get prompt attention. Having the impression that the Government desired to have reputable horsemen in the different parts of the country to purchase horses for the British Government, I addressed a letter in his care, sending the names of six or eight reputable men in the north part of the county of Perth. I got an acknowledgment, but, on inquiry, I find that none of these men were 'consulted at all. It makes a man feel a little bit as. though he weie out of touch with the people when he cannot make headway at all in a matter of this kind. I thought it was well for me to complain to the Government in connection with these matters, because it does not redound to the credit of the Government or strengthen the handling of the resources of the country when members cannot get this information when' they ask oblige those who are desirous of obtaining it. I merely draw attention to the matter so that in the future such a thing may not happen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Agriculture Departmerit has nothing to do with the purchasing of horses either for the British Government or for the Canadian forces. The British Government sent Major General Sir Frederick Benson here to attend to this matter, and the purchasing of horses for the British army was in his hands. If my hon. friend has any fault to find or any complaint to make with regard to the way in which Major General Benson fulfilled his duties, his complaint, should be made to 187	'
the British War Office. I understand that Sir Adam Beck was appointed by the Militia Department to purchase horses that were needed by the Canadian military forces on the other side of the water. It is hard for me to understand why Sir Adam Beck would not send a courteous reply to my hon. friend or to any other member of Parliament who approached him; I certainly think he should have done so. At the same time, Sir Adam Beck is an excellent horseman; he has given a great deal of study and attention to horses, and I have no doubt that the Militia Department in appointing him thought that they were appointing a man who would be as well qualified as any man in Canada to select horses required for the purposes of the military forces that were going overseas.
It is too late to talk about it to-night, but we could give you a history of how these horses were bought.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That may be; fault is
generally found with all these things. I would have thought that a better man for the purpose could not have been selected than Sir Adam Beck, because he is one of the best horsemen in Canada. Moreover, he did the work as a labour of love, making,
I understand, no charge for his services. I regret that my hon. friend had this difficulty in regard to the matter. My hon. friend will understand that the Agriculture Department had nothing to do with this. Purchases of horses for the Canadian forces were made through the Militia Department as part of the equipment of those who were going overseas while purchases for the British Government were made through their direct representative who was sent to Canada for that purpose. I was almost going to tell about a little experience that I myself had in connection with a recommendation I put before Major Genera] Benson, but perhaps I had better not

I think that the minister rather misinterpreted my words, judging from what he said with regard to Sir Adam Beck not giving me a courteous answer. I would not like it to go on record .that I charged him with any lack of courtesy or any act of discourtesy. What I intended to intimate was that apparently he did not know the man whom he himself was supposed to 'have appointed, and, consequently, could" not give me his name and .street address. I think it is worth while

calling the attention of the Government ,to the fact; at least I thought that I could Jiave got the information at Ottawa.

I would remind the hon.
minister that while the Department of Agriculture had not control over the pur-phase of horses for the British Government, or even for the Canadian Government, there was a matter in that connection over which they did have control, - and that was the rejection of diseased United States horses that were scattered broadcast throughout the country, spreading disease among the horses of Canada. When the member fori Missisquoi (Mr. Kay) brought this matter up in the House some time ago in the form of a question, the right hon. Prime Minister answered that it was not in the public interest to give any details. But the livestock commissioner had a bad half hour with the Horse Breeders' Association in Toronto, and there he did give some information that was published widely in the newspapers of the country. He said that some 300 horses had been rejected in Toronto and that 500 horses had been shipped back. The story we hear in Montreal is that 'these horses were not shipped back, but that, Toronto having refused the horses and having declined to have them scattered throughout the country amongst their herds, it was considered that the next best thing was to send them to the province of Quebec-we can stand for pretty nearly anything down there. I am told that the horses were shipped to the province of Quebec and there sold.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We are discussing an item under which this question does not arise. If my hon. friend will bring this matter up under the proper item, we shall have Mr. Bright here, and as he understands the facts of the case, I should be in a better position to give my hon. friend some information.

There will be a good deal of discussion on this item for the development of the live stock industry; it will take a good part of a day to consider. I may tell the minister t'h^t he is going to be asked innumerable questions, particularly with regard to the horse industry-I think I can say from both sides of the House. He is going to be pressed for information that heretofore the Government have intimated they did not desire to give, and I would urge on him as the part of wisdom to bring all the information that he possibly can on the question of horse buying in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman
means the buying of horses for military purposes, I am not the one to ask.
It is the development of the live stock industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The one to ask about it is the Militia * Department.
It is the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: You might as well ask for that information on the railway items as on the- agricultural.
It is connected with the development of the live stock industry, and horse breeding in Canada is a very live stock industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have not bought, a horse.

Somebody ought to be .here to give the information which I know will be asked for. Why should the department aid the Horse Breeders' Association to raise good horses, when the men who raise them cannot find a market for them; and it is intimated that the-Government is responsible, in a measure, for their not getting this market. That matter will be discussed at great length on this live stock item, and I am warning the minister now that when the time comes he will be asked for a lot of information. The Government will have to have some one here to give the information as this question of horse-raising is a very live one all over Canada. I meet occasionally, particularly in Toronto, men who have spent their lives in the horse industry and I know that the horse breeders of all Canada are very much perturbed over the manner in which purchasing of horses for war purposes has been managed. I am not referring now to the purchase of old horses, or anything of that kind, but to something of a larger scope than that, although that may, perhaps, be discusse.d incidentally. The different live stock associations throughout Canada, who started on a very small scale and have been gradually extending their efforts until they have come to a point where they control one of the greatest industries on this continent, feel that during the past year or so they have not had an opportunity to supply all the needs that were being supplied through this Government, directly or indirectly, for war or other purposes. I would suggest that certain items be passed to-night, on

the understanding that members will be free to discuss any item on those that re-, main.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will allow the large item to stand, with the mental reservation that we can discuss any minor item on it. We have always done that. I suppose I should thank my hon. friend for the warning he has given me, because they say that forewarned is forearmed. I am always willing and anxious to give the committee any information in my power, but it is hardly necessary to point out to an old parliamentarian like my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) that information should be-sought from the p-roper quarters with regard to estimates before the House, and if my hon. friend wants information about the purchase of horses for military purposes in Canada the Agricultural Department is not the one to go to for that information, because the Agricultural Department has not that information, within its possession in the same intimate way as the department that has purchased those horses. These horses have been bought for war purposes, and it would be as improper to ask the Marine Department as to ask the Agricultural Department, as neither of them had anything to do with the question.

You are speaking of the horse marines.
Mr: HAZEN: The horse marine used to be a very important element in the navy, but he does not amount to much now.

I would suggest to the
minister that he interrogate the Militia Department in order to get some information, because he can see that the development of the live stock industry depends on the sale there is for its product, and where the Department of Agriculture is encouraging the production of horses, it is hardly fair to the members to say that that Department is not in a position to give information as to the reasons for the horse breeders not being able to sell their horses. It is a case where the Government must be held responsible as a unit, and some member of the Government ought to give the information when money is being voted/ to develop the industry.

Would the minister tell the
committee what is being done with the King's horse Amner? I am sure that the House and the country are all very grateful to His Majesty for presenting this horse to Canada, and it would be of great interest to us to know what is going to be done with him this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That horse has been placed in charge of the Canadian Thoroughbred Horse Society, under conditions that have been agreed on between the Department of Agriculture and this association. They keep him entirely free of charge for a period of one year, and the money received from his services, on a scale of fees agreed to, is to be devoted to prizes, to be given at different fairs throughout the country for thoroughbred animals, and horses suitable for use as remounts. The information can be given on the live stock item, or I can send it to my hon. friend.
Where is the horse at present?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: At present he is at Oakville, near Toronto, which is the headquarters of this breeders' association.
He will be kept in Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He will be sent to different places. I presume he will be sent to Quebec.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hr. Hazen, the House adjourned at 11.40 p.m.
